problems.intuition: Embedding length often reflects things like word frequency or text length rather than meaning, while direction carries the semantics. Dividing the dot product by both norms keeps only direction, and after normalising rows, a whole similarity matrix is a single matrix product.
problems.whyItWorks: The dot product equals the product of the norms times the cosine of the angle, so dividing by the norms leaves a pure angle between −1 and 1. For unit vectors the squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus twice the cosine, so ranking by cosine and by Euclidean distance agree once the vectors are normalised. Scaling either vector leaves the value unchanged.
approach: Compute each row's L2 norm — the length to be removed
Divide each row by its norm, with a small floor — unit vectors, safe for zero rows
Multiply normalised queries by normalised keys transposed — every dot product is now a cosine
Sort scores in descending order and take the top k — the nearest neighbours by angle
problems.time: O(m·n·d) for m queries, n items and width d
problems.space: O(m·n) for the similarity matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def cosine_matrix(A, B, eps=1e-12):
    na = np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    nb = np.linalg.norm(B, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    An = A / np.maximum(na, eps)
    Bn = B / np.maximum(nb, eps)
    return An @ Bn.T

def top_k_neighbors(q, E, k):
    s = cosine_matrix(q[None, :], E)[0]
    idx = np.argsort(-s)[:k]
    return idx, s[idx]
dryRun: cos(a, b) = a·b / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)
Normalise: â = a / max(‖a‖, ε)
S = Â B̂ᵀ   (all pairwise cosines)
For unit vectors: ‖â − b̂‖² = 2 − 2 cos(a, b)
Cosine distance = 1 − cos(a, b)
problems.description: Semantic search, retrieval for RAG, deduplication and clustering of text embeddings, and any model whose embeddings are trained with a cosine or contrastive objective.

examples.input: Why use cosine similarity instead of the raw dot product?
examples.output: The dot product grows with vector length, so long vectors look similar to everything. Cosine removes length and compares direction only.

examples.input: Is cosine distance a true metric?
examples.output: No. 1 − cos can violate the triangle inequality. The angle itself is a metric, and the Euclidean distance between normalised vectors is too.

examples.input: How do you speed up cosine search over millions of vectors?
examples.output: Normalise once, then maximum inner product search with an approximate index works directly, since cosine becomes a dot product.

constraints: Epsilon floor for zero-norm vectors
Number of neighbours k
Whether embeddings are pre-normalised
edgeCases: Zero vectors divide by zero without the epsilon floor, and then give similarity 0
A cosine score is not calibrated; thresholds depend on the embedding model
Full argsort is O(n log n); real systems use partial selection or an approximate index

problems.title: Cross-Attention (Encoder-Decoder)
problems.summary: Let each decoder position look up information in the encoder output: queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder.
problems.bruteForce: Decoder-only language models have no separate source, so they use self-attention over a concatenated prompt instead. Very long sources make the target-by-source score matrix expensive.
problems.intuition: Self-attention lets a sequence read itself; cross-attention lets one sequence read another. The decoder state asks "which source words do I need to produce the next word?", and the encoder outputs answer with keys to match and values to hand over. The source length and target length are independent, so the weight matrix is rectangular, one row per target position and one column per source position.
problems.whyItWorks: The encoder compresses the source once; the decoder can then consult any source position at every step with content-based weights instead of squeezing the source into one fixed vector. Keys and values are computed once per source and reused for every generated token. A padding mask sets the scores of padded source columns to −∞ so they receive exactly zero weight.
approach: Project decoder states to queries — the decoder is the one asking
Project encoder outputs to keys and values — the source supplies what to match and what to give
Score every target-source pair with Q·Kᵀ/√d_k — rectangular matrix, scaled to keep softmax healthy
Mask padded source columns with −∞ — padding must receive zero weight
Softmax each row and multiply by V — each target position gets a weighted average of source values
problems.time: O(T_dec·T_enc·d) for target length T_dec, source length T_enc and width d
problems.space: O(T_dec·T_enc) for the attention matrix; K and V (O(T_enc·d)) can be cached across decoding steps
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(s):
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_attention(Xd, Xe, Wq, Wk, Wv, src_mask=None):
    Q = Xd @ Wq                  # queries: decoder
    K, V = Xe @ Wk, Xe @ Wv      # keys, values: encoder
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
    if src_mask is not None:     # True = real token, False = pad
        scores = np.where(src_mask[None, :], scores, -np.inf)
    A = softmax(scores)
    return A @ V, A
dryRun: Q = X_dec·W_q   (T_dec × d_k)
K = X_enc·W_k,  V = X_enc·W_v   (T_enc × d_k, T_enc × d_v)
S = Q·Kᵀ / √d_k   (T_dec × T_enc)
Padding: S[i, j] = −∞ where source position j is padding
A = softmax(S) row-wise, so each row sums to 1
Output = A·V   (T_dec × d_v)
problems.description: Translation, summarisation, speech recognition and any encoder-decoder model where the output must be conditioned on a separate input sequence, including image-to-text models whose encoder outputs are patches.

examples.input: Where do Q, K and V come from in cross-attention?
examples.output: Queries come from the decoder's current hidden states; keys and values come from the encoder's final outputs. The attention matrix is therefore target length by source length.

examples.input: Why can encoder keys and values be cached during generation?
examples.output: The source does not change while decoding, so its keys and values are computed once and reused at every step; only the new query is computed each step.

examples.input: Does cross-attention need a causal mask?
examples.output: No. The decoder may look at the whole source; causality applies only to the decoder's self-attention over its own previous outputs. A padding mask on the source is what it needs.

constraints: Key/query dimension d_k (sets the scale √d_k)
Number of heads (this code is a single head)
Source padding mask (needed whenever sources in a batch differ in length)
Attention dropout
edgeCases: Forgetting the source padding mask lets the decoder attend to padding tokens
A source that is entirely padding gives a fully masked row and NaN; real batches contain at least one real token
Queries must come from the decoder; swapping the roles gives a source-by-target matrix instead
This is one head with no output projection, residual or layer norm, which a real decoder layer adds

problems.title: K-Fold Cross-Validation
problems.summary: Estimate generalisation by splitting the data into k folds, training on k − 1 of them and scoring on the held-out one, rotating through all k.
problems.bruteForce: Skip plain shuffled k-fold for time series (use forward chaining) and grouped data (use group k-fold), and avoid it when one fit is so expensive that k fits are impractical.
problems.intuition: A single train/validation split wastes data and its score depends on which rows landed where. Rotating the held-out fold means every row is used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times, so the averaged score is steadier and the spread shows how fragile it is.
problems.whyItWorks: Each fold's score is an unbiased-ish estimate of error on unseen data because the model never saw those rows. Averaging k such estimates reduces the variance caused by one lucky or unlucky split. It is slightly pessimistic because each model trains on only a fraction (k − 1)/k of the data.
approach: Shuffle the row indices with a fixed seed — so folds are not ordered by collection time and runs repeat
Split the indices into k nearly equal folds — each row lands in exactly one fold
For each fold, train on the other k − 1 — the model must never see its validation rows
Score the held-out fold — gives one honest estimate per fold
Report mean and spread — the spread shows how stable the estimate is
problems.time: k times the cost of one fit, plus O(n) for the splits
problems.space: O(n) for the index folds
dryRun: folds F₁ … F_k partition {1 … n}, sizes differ by at most 1
ŵ₋ᵢ = fit(data outside Fᵢ)
CV = (1/k) Σᵢ score(ŵ₋ᵢ, Fᵢ)
spread = std of the k fold scores
problems.description: Comparing models or hyperparameters on small to medium datasets when a single hold-out set would be too noisy or too costly in data.

examples.input: Why k = 5 or 10 and not leave-one-out?
examples.output: Leave-one-out has low bias but the n models are highly correlated, so the estimate has high variance and costs n fits; 5 or 10 folds is a good compromise.

examples.input: Why use stratified k-fold for classification?
examples.output: It keeps the class proportions in every fold, so rare classes do not vanish from some validation folds.

examples.input: How do you tune hyperparameters without fooling yourself?
examples.output: Use nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks hyperparameters and an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure.

constraints: Number of folds k (5 or 10 is typical; larger k means less bias and higher cost)
Shuffling and random seed
Stratification for classification (keeps class ratios per fold)
Scoring metric
edgeCases: Fitting preprocessing (scaler, imputer, feature selection) on all data before splitting leaks into the folds
Using the CV score to tune many hyperparameters and then reporting it as final performance overfits to the folds
Random folds on time-ordered or grouped data leak the future or the same entity

problems.title: Data Augmentation
problems.summary: Create new training examples on the fly by applying random, label-preserving transformations such as flips and crops to the existing images.
problems.bruteForce: Not on validation or test data (only deterministic preprocessing there), and not with transforms that change the label such as flipping text or digits.
problems.intuition: A flipped or slightly shifted cat is still a cat, so each random transform shows the model the same label under a new appearance. This teaches the invariances you care about without collecting more data, and it makes memorising exact pixel patterns much harder. Normalisation is applied last, with fixed statistics, so training and test inputs are on the same scale.
problems.whyItWorks: Augmentation enlarges the effective training distribution along directions where the true label does not change, which acts as a data-dependent regulariser and reduces variance. It only helps if the transform really preserves the label; a flipped digit or a crop that removes the object injects label noise.
approach: Draw the random decisions (flip or not, crop offsets) — each epoch sees a different version
Flip the width axis when the coin says so — mirror symmetry preserves most labels
Slice a random crop of the target size — shifts and rescales what the model sees
Subtract the channel mean and divide by the channel std — same scaling at train and test
problems.time: O(C·size²) per image
problems.space: O(C·size²) for the output; flips and crops are views
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def augment(x, rng, size, mean, std):
    # x: (C, H, W) image; returns (C, size, size)
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        x = x[:, :, ::-1]
    top = rng.integers(0, x.shape[1] - size + 1)
    left = rng.integers(0, x.shape[2] - size + 1)
    x = x[:, top:top + size, left:left + size]
    return (x - mean[:, None, None]) / std[:, None, None]
dryRun: Flip: x'[c,i,j] = x[c,i,W−1−j]  with probability 0.5
Crop: x'[c,i,j] = x[c,t+i,l+j],  t, l drawn at random
Normalise: x''[c] = (x'[c] − μ_c) / σ_c  per channel
Label unchanged: y' = y
problems.description: Small or medium image datasets and any model prone to overfitting, with transforms matched to the task's real invariances.

examples.input: Why does augmentation reduce overfitting?
examples.output: It makes the model see many label-preserving variants of each image, so it cannot rely on exact pixels and learns the intended invariances.

examples.input: Should you augment at test time?
examples.output: Normally no, only deterministic preprocessing; test-time augmentation is a separate technique that averages predictions.

examples.input: How do you choose augmentations?
examples.output: Pick transforms the label is truly invariant to in your domain and validate that they help.

constraints: Flip probability
Crop size (and padding or scale range in practice)
Strength of colour or geometric jitter (not modelled here)
Normalisation mean and std
edgeCases: Augmenting validation or test data hides the true generalisation
Transforms that change the label (flipped digits, over-aggressive crops) add noise
Normalise with training statistics, not per-batch statistics
This sketch only flips, crops and normalises; real pipelines add scale, rotation and colour changes

problems.title: Data Leakage
problems.summary: Information from the validation or test data leaks into training, so the measured score looks better than real-world performance.
problems.bruteForce: Not a technique to apply but a failure to avoid. Statistics from the unlabelled target domain are legitimately used in transductive or domain-adaptation setups, if documented as such.
problems.intuition: Anything computed with the test rows, such as scaling statistics, imputation values, selected features or even a duplicated row, lets the model peek at the answer sheet. The rule is simple: every data-dependent step is part of the model, so fit it on the training fold only and merely apply it to held-out data.
problems.whyItWorks: A fair evaluation simulates deployment, where future data and labels are unseen when the model is built. Fitting a transform on the training split and reusing its parameters mimics that exactly, whereas fitting on all data lets validation rows influence the parameters they are scored with.
approach: Split first, before any data-dependent step — the test rows stay unseen
Fit scaler, imputer and feature selector on the training rows only — these are part of the model
Apply the fitted transform to validation and test rows — same parameters, no refitting
Do all of this inside each cross-validation fold — a pipeline object enforces it
Check for duplicates, group overlap and target-derived features — other common leaks
problems.time: O(n·d) for the scaling; the cost is a wrong estimate, not compute
problems.space: O(d) for the fitted statistics
dryRun: Correct: θ̂ = fit(X_train), Z = transform(X; θ̂)
Leaky: θ̂ = fit(X_train ∪ X_test)
Standardise: z = (x − μ̂) / σ̂, using train μ̂ and σ̂ only
Leaky stats shrink the train/test shift, so the test set looks easier
problems.description: Audit every pipeline before trusting a metric, especially when the score looks too good, or when preprocessing and feature selection precede the train-test split or cross-validation.

examples.input: Your model scores very well offline but poorly in production. What do you check first?
examples.output: Leakage: preprocessing or feature selection fit on all data, target-derived features, duplicates across splits, or a split that ignores time or groups.

examples.input: How do you prevent preprocessing leakage in cross-validation?
examples.output: Put the transforms and the model in one pipeline so each fold fits the transforms on its own training part only.

examples.input: Is scaling before the split really a problem?
examples.output: It is a mild leak since only means and variances cross over, but selection, imputation and target encoding can leak far more.

constraints: Split strategy (random, time-based or grouped) that matches deployment
Where preprocessing is fitted (inside each fold with a pipeline)
edgeCases: Selecting features with the labels on all data before cross-validation inflates scores even on pure noise
Random splits of time series let the model train on the future
Duplicate or near-duplicate rows (or the same user) in both train and test
Features computed after the outcome, such as a status flag set once the event happens

problems.title: DBSCAN
problems.summary: Grow clusters from dense regions: a point with enough neighbours inside radius eps is a core point, clusters are chains of overlapping core neighbourhoods, and points reachable from no core are noise.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when clusters have very different densities (one eps cannot fit both), in high dimensions where distances concentrate, or for big data without a spatial index (this code is quadratic).
problems.intuition: A cluster is a region where you can keep walking from point to point without ever stepping across a gap bigger than eps in a crowd of at least min_pts. This defines clusters by connectivity of density rather than by distance to a centre, so it finds crescents and rings and needs no cluster count, and it can say that a point belongs nowhere.
problems.whyItWorks: Core points that lie within eps of each other are density-connected, and connectivity among core points is an equivalence relation, so each connected component is one well-defined cluster. Border points (non-core, but within eps of a core) attach to a neighbouring cluster, and everything else is labelled noise.
approach: Compute all pairwise distances and eps-neighbourhoods — the definition of density is neighbour count
Mark points with at least min_pts neighbours as core — only these may grow clusters
Visit unlabelled core points in order and start a new cluster at each — one seed per connected component
Flood-fill from a core point through its neighbours, expanding only through other core points — border points join but do not spread the cluster
Leave unreached points as −1 — noise is a legitimate outcome
problems.time: O(n²) with the distance matrix here; O(n log n) with a KD/ball tree in low dimensions
problems.space: O(n²) for the distance matrix here; O(n) with a spatial index
dryRun: N_eps(i) = { j : ‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖ ≤ eps }  (includes i itself)
Core: |N_eps(i)| ≥ min_pts
j is directly reachable from i if i is core and j ∈ N_eps(i)
Cluster = core points linked by reachability, plus their borders
Noise = points not reachable from any core, label −1
problems.description: Non-convex clusters, unknown number of clusters, data with outliers you want flagged, and low-dimensional spatial or geographic data.

examples.input: What are core, border and noise points?
examples.output: Core points have at least min_pts points within eps, border points are within eps of a core but not core themselves, and noise is everything else.

examples.input: How do you choose eps?
examples.output: Plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour sorted ascending and pick the knee, then sanity-check the clusters.

examples.input: Why can DBSCAN beat k-means?
examples.output: It needs no cluster count, finds arbitrary shapes, and marks outliers, whereas k-means assumes compact, similar-sized convex clusters and assigns every point.

constraints: eps — neighbourhood radius; read it off a k-distance plot
min_pts — density threshold; a common start is twice the dimension
metric — Euclidean by default, but any distance works
edgeCases: Features must be scaled first, otherwise eps means nothing
Border points touching two clusters go to whichever is reached first, so results depend on row order
Mixed-density data: a single eps merges the dense clusters or drops the sparse ones as noise
min_pts counts the point itself, so conventions differ between libraries

problems.title: Decision Tree
problems.summary: Predict by asking a chain of yes/no questions on single features. The tree is grown greedily, choosing at each node the split that makes the two child groups as pure as possible.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a single deep tree when you need stable predictions or smooth boundaries: small data changes flip splits, and axis-aligned cuts approximate diagonal boundaries badly.
problems.intuition: A tree carves feature space into axis-aligned boxes and predicts the majority class of each box. Growing it is just a repeated search: try every threshold on every feature and keep the one that most reduces impurity, then recurse on each side as if it were a new problem.
problems.whyItWorks: Each split can never increase the weighted impurity, because the parent is a mix of its children. So deeper trees fit the training data ever better, which is also the danger: with no depth limit the tree memorises noise. The greedy choice is not globally optimal, but it is cheap and works well in practice.
approach: Compute the Gini impurity of the node — it measures how mixed the classes are
Stop if depth is used up or the node is pure — this limits overfitting
Try midpoints between sorted values of each feature — these are all distinct splits
Score each split by weighted child impurity — pick the lowest cost
Recurse on left and right subsets — each child is a smaller copy of the problem
Predict by walking from the root to a leaf — each test sends the sample left or right
problems.time: O(d · n² ) naive per node as written; O(d · n log n) per level with sorting and running counts
problems.space: O(n) for the data plus O(nodes) for the tree
dryRun: Gini(S) = 1 − Σₖ pₖ²,  pₖ = share of class k in S
Entropy(S) = −Σₖ pₖ · log₂ pₖ
Split cost = (|L|/|S|)·Gini(L) + (|R|/|S|)·Gini(R)
L = {x : xⱼ ≤ t},  R = {x : xⱼ > t}
Gain = Gini(S) − Split cost
Leaf prediction = argmaxₖ pₖ
problems.description: Interpretable models on tabular data with mixed scales and non-linear interactions, and as the base learner for forests and boosting.

examples.input: Gini or entropy?
examples.output: Both measure impurity and usually pick near-identical splits; Gini avoids the logarithm so it is slightly faster.

examples.input: How do you stop a tree from overfitting?
examples.output: Limit depth, require a minimum leaf size, or grow fully and prune with cost-complexity; or average many trees in a forest.

examples.input: Do trees need feature scaling?
examples.output: No. Splits compare a feature to a threshold, so any monotonic rescaling gives the same tree.

constraints: max_depth — main control of over/underfitting
min_samples_leaf — forbids tiny, noisy leaves
criterion — Gini or entropy, rarely matters
ccp_alpha — cost-complexity pruning strength
edgeCases: Unlimited depth reaches 100% training accuracy and overfits
Split search favours features with many distinct values
Equal-gain splits are tied: sklearn breaks ties by a random feature order, so deep trees can differ from this code
Predictions are piecewise constant, so a tree cannot extrapolate

problems.title: Depthwise Separable Convolution
problems.summary: Split a standard convolution into a per-channel spatial filter (depthwise) followed by a 1×1 convolution that mixes channels (pointwise).
problems.bruteForce: When compute is plentiful and accuracy matters most; the factorised layer is less expressive and depthwise operations can run inefficiently on some hardware despite fewer operations.
problems.intuition: A standard convolution does two jobs at once: it looks at spatial neighbourhoods and it mixes channels, with a separate weight for every pair. Factoring these apart gives each channel its own small spatial filter, then mixes channels per pixel. The product of two cheap steps approximates the expensive joint one, and the saving grows with the number of channels and the kernel area.
problems.whyItWorks: The factorised layer is a low-rank structure on the full kernel: the spatial pattern is shared across all output channels instead of being learned separately for each. Natural images often have features where spatial and cross-channel structure can be treated separately, so far fewer parameters and multiplications lose little accuracy.
approach: Pad the input like an ordinary convolution — same output-size rules apply
For each position, take the patch of every channel separately — channels are not mixed yet
Multiply each channel's patch by that channel's own k×k filter and sum — the depthwise step
Mix channels at each pixel with a F×C matrix — the pointwise 1×1 step produces F maps
problems.time: O(N·oH·oW·C·(kH·kW + F))
problems.space: O(N·C·oH·oW) for the intermediate maps
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def depthwise_separable(x, dw, pw, stride=1, pad=0):
    # x: (N,C,H,W)  dw: (C,kh,kw)  pw: (F,C)
    x = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    _, kh, kw = dw.shape
    oh = (h - kh) // stride + 1
    ow = (w - kw) // stride + 1
    mid = np.zeros((n, c, oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
            patch = x[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw]
            mid[:, :, i, j] = (patch * dw).sum((2, 3))
    return np.einsum("nchw,fc->nfhw", mid, pw)
dryRun: Depthwise: m[n,c,i,j] = Σ_u Σ_v d[c,u,v] · x[n,c,si+u,sj+v]
Pointwise: out[n,f,i,j] = Σ_c p[f,c] · m[n,c,i,j]
Standard parameters: F·C·k²;  separable: C·k² + F·C
Cost ratio (params): 1/F + 1/k²
problems.description: Mobile and edge models (MobileNet, Xception, EfficientNet) where parameters and compute are limited.

examples.input: How does a depthwise separable convolution save parameters?
examples.output: It uses C·k² spatial weights plus F·C mixing weights instead of F·C·k² for the full kernel.

examples.input: What does the depthwise step do?
examples.output: It filters each input channel independently with its own spatial kernel, so it mixes no information across channels.

examples.input: What does the pointwise step do?
examples.output: A 1×1 convolution that linearly combines channels at every position, producing the output channels.

constraints: Kernel size of the depthwise filter
Stride and padding
Output channels F of the pointwise layer
Depth multiplier (not modelled; this uses one filter per channel)
edgeCases: Fewer multiply-adds do not always mean faster inference; memory-bound depthwise kernels can be slow
Normalisation and a nonlinearity between the two steps matter in real blocks; this sketch has none
Biases are omitted in this sketch
Compare parameter counts with equal accuracy, not with equal width

problems.title: Diffusion Forward (Noising) Process
problems.summary: Gradually turn data into Gaussian noise by adding a little noise at each step, and jump straight to any step t with one closed-form sample.
problems.bruteForce: Sampling new data, which needs the learned reverse process. The forward process alone is fixed and has no parameters to learn.
problems.intuition: Each noising step shrinks the signal slightly and adds fresh Gaussian noise, and a chain of Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian. Their combined effect collapses into a single draw with a scaled copy of the data plus noise, so training can pick a random t and corrupt x₀ in one shot instead of simulating t steps.
problems.whyItWorks: Each step maps x to a Gaussian with mean √(1−β)·x and variance β. A Gaussian pushed through a linear map plus independent Gaussian noise stays Gaussian, so the mean shrinks by √(1−βₜ) each step and the variance obeys v ← (1−βₜ)·v + βₜ. Solving these recursions gives mean √ᾱₜ x₀ and variance 1 − ᾱₜ, and variance one is preserved at the noise limit. This code uses a linear schedule; other schedules are common.
approach: Choose a noise schedule β₁ … β_T — how much noise each step adds
Form ᾱₜ as the running product of (1 − βₜ) — the fraction of signal variance that survives to step t
Draw ε ~ N(0, I) — the only randomness
Output √ᾱₜ · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ) · ε — a sample of q(xₜ | x₀) in one step
Optionally iterate √(1−βₜ) x + √βₜ ε — the same distribution by single steps
problems.time: O(d) per sample at any t, versus O(t·d) by iterating
problems.space: O(T) for the schedule and O(d) per sample
dryRun: q(xₜ | xₜ₋₁) = N(√(1−βₜ) xₜ₋₁, βₜ I)
αₜ = 1 − βₜ,   ᾱₜ = Πₛ≤ₜ αₛ
q(xₜ | x₀) = N(√ᾱₜ x₀, (1 − ᾱₜ) I)
xₜ = √ᾱₜ x₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ) ε,   ε ~ N(0, I)
Recursions: mₜ = √αₜ mₜ₋₁,   vₜ = αₜ vₜ₋₁ + βₜ
x₀ = (xₜ − √(1 − ᾱₜ) ε) / √ᾱₜ
SNR(t) = ᾱₜ / (1 − ᾱₜ)
problems.description: Building the training pairs for denoising diffusion models, where a random t and fresh noise corrupt each clean example, and analysing a noise schedule such as its signal-to-noise ratio.

examples.input: Why can we sample xₜ directly from x₀?
examples.output: Each step is Gaussian and linear in the previous state, so composing t of them gives one Gaussian with mean √ᾱₜ x₀ and variance 1 − ᾱₜ.

examples.input: Why scale the signal by √(1−βₜ) instead of only adding noise?
examples.output: The shrinkage keeps the total variance bounded, so the chain ends near a standard normal instead of growing without limit.

examples.input: What does the network learn in DDPM?
examples.output: It predicts the noise ε from xₜ and t, which is equivalent to estimating x₀ using the closed-form relation between the two.

constraints: Number of steps T
Schedule endpoints β₁ and β_T, or the schedule family (linear, cosine)
Data scaling, usually to [−1, 1]
edgeCases: Indexing off by one: array position t here is step t+1 of the maths
The final ᾱ_T must be near zero or the terminal distribution is not standard normal
The equivalence with iterating holds in distribution, not sample by sample for the same ε

problems.title: Direct Preference Optimisation Loss
problems.summary: Fine-tune a language model on pairs of preferred and rejected responses by pushing up the log-probability gap between them, measured relative to a frozen reference model, with no separate reward model or reinforcement learning loop.
problems.bruteForce: When preferences must be gathered online from the current policy, when a reusable reward model is needed for ranking or filtering, or when the preference data is far from the reference model's distribution.
problems.intuition: DPO treats β·log(π/π_ref) as an implicit reward: how much more the tuned model likes a response than the reference does. The loss is a logistic loss on the difference of that implicit reward between the chosen and rejected response, so it raises the chosen response and lowers the rejected one relative to the reference. Anchoring to the reference is what keeps the model from drifting arbitrarily far.
problems.whyItWorks: The KL-regularised reward maximisation problem has a closed-form optimal policy, which can be inverted to express any reward as a log-ratio of policy to reference. Substituting that into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood cancels the intractable normaliser, leaving a loss that depends only on sequence log-probabilities. The gradient weights each pair by how wrongly the implicit reward currently orders it.
approach: Compute sequence log-probabilities of the chosen and rejected responses under the policy and the frozen reference — the four quantities the loss needs
Subtract reference from policy for each response — the log-ratio is the implicit reward up to β
Take the chosen-minus-rejected difference and scale by β — the preference margin
Apply −log σ(margin) and average over pairs — the Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood
Backpropagate into the policy only — the reference stays frozen
problems.time: O(N) given the log-probabilities; the real cost is two forward passes (policy and reference) per response
problems.space: O(N) for the margins; the reference model's weights must also be held in memory
dryRun: Implicit reward: r(x, y) = β · log( π(y|x) / π_ref(y|x) )
Margin: m = β·[(log π(y_w) − log π_ref(y_w))
− (log π(y_l) − log π_ref(y_l))]
Loss: L = −mean over pairs of log σ(m)
∂L/∂log π(y_w) = −β σ(−m) / N,  ∂L/∂log π(y_l) = +β σ(−m) / N
y_w: preferred (winner),  y_l: rejected (loser),  N: pairs
problems.description: Aligning an instruction-tuned model with a static dataset of preference pairs when a simple, stable supervised-style training loop is preferred over PPO.

examples.input: How does DPO avoid training a reward model?
examples.output: It reparameterises the reward as a log-ratio of policy to reference, so the preference likelihood can be written directly in terms of the policy. Training the policy on that likelihood implicitly fits the reward.

examples.input: What does β control?
examples.output: It scales the log-ratio reward, so it sets how strongly the policy is tied to the reference. A larger β penalises movement away from the reference more and gives smaller updates for a given log-ratio gap.

examples.input: How does DPO relate to RLHF with PPO?
examples.output: Both target the same KL-regularised reward objective. PPO learns an explicit reward and samples from the policy online; DPO optimises a closed-form loss on a fixed dataset of preference pairs.

constraints: β (strength of the pull toward the reference; larger keeps the policy closer)
Learning rate (usually very small for fine-tuning)
Reference model (usually the supervised fine-tuned checkpoint)
Preference dataset quality and size
edgeCases: Inputs must be sequence-level log-probs (summed over response tokens), computed with the same prompt formatting
Reference log-probs are constants; backpropagating into the reference is a bug
Both chosen and rejected log-probs can fall during training; DPO constrains only their gap
This code returns gradients with respect to the log-probs; a real model backpropagates them into its parameters, and long sequences make the log-probs very negative

problems.title: Dropout
problems.summary: During training, randomly zero each activation with probability p and scale the survivors by 1 / (1 − p); at inference do nothing.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the model underfits or data is plentiful, and be careful alongside batch norm, where the two interact badly. Always disable it at evaluation.
problems.intuition: Randomly silencing units stops any neuron from relying on specific partners, so the network must spread useful information across many features. Scaling the survivors at training time keeps the expected activation unchanged, so no adjustment is needed at inference.
problems.whyItWorks: Each training step samples a different thinned sub-network, so the full network behaves like an average over exponentially many models that share weights, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. The 1 / (1 − p) factor (inverted dropout) makes the expected output equal the input.
approach: Sample a keep mask with probability 1 − p per element — decides which units survive this step
Divide the mask by 1 − p — keeps the expected activation equal to the input
Multiply input by the scaled mask — dropped units output zero
Reuse the same scaled mask in the backward pass — dropped units must receive zero gradient
Return the input unchanged in eval mode — inference is deterministic
problems.time: O(n) for n activations
problems.space: O(n) for the stored mask
dryRun: mᵢ ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)  (1 = keep)
Train: y = x ⊙ m / (1 − p)
E[y] = x  (inverted scaling)
Eval: y = x
Backward: ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y ⊙ m / (1 − p)
problems.description: Large fully connected layers or models that overfit, and inside transformers on attention and feed-forward outputs.

examples.input: What is inverted dropout?
examples.output: Scaling surviving activations by 1 / (1 − p) at training time so the expected output equals the input and inference needs no change.

examples.input: Why does dropout regularise?
examples.output: It prevents co-adaptation of units and approximates averaging over many thinned networks.

examples.input: What happens to gradients of dropped units?
examples.output: They are zero for that step, because the same mask multiplies the upstream gradient.

constraints: Drop probability p (higher means stronger regularisation)
Where to place it (after which layers)
Variant (element-wise dropout, spatial dropout for channels)
edgeCases: Leaving dropout on at inference makes predictions random
Mixing up p (drop probability) with keep probability gives the wrong scale
The mask must be reused in backward, not resampled
The mask here comes from NumPy's generator, so it cannot match torch's random mask element for element

problems.title: Early Stopping
problems.summary: Watch the validation loss during training and stop when it has not improved for a set number of epochs, then keep the weights from the best epoch. Training length becomes a regularised hyperparameter chosen automatically.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the validation set is tiny or noisy (the stopping point becomes random), and note that the chosen epoch is tuned on validation data, so report results on a separate test set.
problems.intuition: Training loss usually keeps falling, but past some point the model starts fitting noise and validation loss turns upward. Number of epochs therefore acts as a capacity knob: early on the model is simple, later it is flexible. Stopping near the validation minimum buys a simple model for free, and patience stops a noisy blip from ending training too soon.
problems.whyItWorks: For gradient descent from small initial weights, the weights grow gradually away from zero, so fewer steps restrict the effective model size, similar in effect to an L2 penalty. The validation curve estimates generalisation error, and the rule picks the epoch where that estimate was lowest, with patience trading a small delay for robustness to noise.
approach: Hold out a validation set the model never trains on — it measures generalisation
After each epoch, evaluate validation loss — the signal for when overfitting begins
If it beats the best by more than min_delta, record it, save the weights and reset the counter — progress is real
Otherwise increment the patience counter — a few bad epochs may just be noise
Stop when the counter reaches patience and restore the saved weights — the last epochs were overfit
problems.time: O(1) per epoch for the check; the cost is the validation pass itself
problems.space: O(P) to keep a copy of the best weights (this snippet tracks indices only)
dryRun: best = min over epochs so far of val_loss
Improvement at epoch t: val_loss[t] < best − min_delta
wait = 0 on improvement, otherwise wait ← wait + 1
Stop at the first epoch where wait ≥ patience
Return the weights saved at the best epoch
problems.description: Neural networks and boosted ensembles trained iteratively, especially when you cannot afford to tune the epoch count by hand.

examples.input: Why is early stopping a regulariser?
examples.output: Fewer gradient steps keep weights near their small initial values, limiting effective capacity, much as a weight penalty does.

examples.input: What does patience do?
examples.output: It tolerates a few non-improving epochs so a noisy validation curve does not end training prematurely.

examples.input: Which data decides when to stop, and which reports the final score?
examples.output: Validation data decides the stopping epoch; a separate untouched test set gives the final unbiased estimate.

constraints: patience — epochs to wait without improvement
min_delta — smallest change that counts as improvement
monitor — the validation metric (loss or a score) and whether lower or higher is better
restore_best_weights — whether to roll back to the best epoch
edgeCases: Patience too small stops on noise; too large wastes compute and overfits
Stopping on training loss never triggers, since it keeps decreasing
The validation set is reused to choose the epoch, so it no longer gives an unbiased final score
Without restoring the best weights you keep the over-trained final model

problems.title: Elastic Net via Coordinate Descent
problems.summary: Linear regression with a mix of L1 and L2 penalties, solved by cycling through coordinates and updating one weight at a time with a soft-threshold. The L1 part zeroes weights; the L2 part stabilises groups of correlated features.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you want unbiased estimates of the large coefficients (the penalty shrinks them), when features are unscaled, or when you need coefficient standard errors and p-values.
problems.intuition: With all other weights held fixed, the objective in one weight is a one-dimensional problem whose answer is closed form: take the plain least-squares fit to the current residual, shrink it toward zero by the L1 amount (stopping at exactly zero) and divide by a factor that includes the L2 penalty. Cycling over coordinates repeats this until nothing moves.
problems.whyItWorks: The squared loss is smooth and convex and the penalty is convex and separable across coordinates, which is the case where coordinate descent provably converges to the global minimum. Each one-dimensional subproblem is solved exactly by soft-thresholding, so the objective never increases.
approach: Start at w = 0 with residual r = y — the exact solution once α is large enough
For coordinate j compute its correlation with the partial residual, adding back its own contribution — the least-squares target for wⱼ alone
Soft-threshold by αρ and divide by zⱼ + α(1 − ρ) — the closed-form minimiser of the one-dimensional problem
Update the residual by the change in wⱼ — keeps each step O(n) instead of recomputing Xw
Sweep all coordinates until the largest change is below tol — all coordinate steps are small only at the minimum
problems.time: O(iters·n·d) with the residual trick; each sweep costs O(n·d)
problems.space: O(n·d) for the data, O(n + d) extra
dryRun: min over w of (1/2n)‖y − Xw‖² + αρ‖w‖₁ + ½α(1−ρ)‖w‖²
rⱼ = y − Σₖ≠ⱼ xₖ wₖ  (partial residual)
zⱼ = ‖xⱼ‖² / n,  ρⱼ = xⱼᵀ rⱼ / n
S(a, t) = sign(a) · max(|a| − t, 0)
wⱼ ← S(ρⱼ, αρ) / (zⱼ + α(1 − ρ))
ρ = 1 gives lasso, ρ = 0 gives ridge
problems.description: Many correlated features where lasso picks one arbitrarily, p larger than n, automatic feature selection with stable grouping, and large sparse problems where coordinate descent is fast.

examples.input: Why use elastic net instead of lasso?
examples.output: Among correlated features lasso tends to pick one at random, while the L2 term makes elastic net share weight across the group and also lets it keep more than n features when p is larger than n.

examples.input: What does the soft-threshold do?
examples.output: It shrinks the least-squares coordinate estimate toward zero by the L1 amount and sets it exactly to zero when it is smaller than that amount, which is how sparsity arises.

examples.input: Why does coordinate descent converge here?
examples.output: The loss is smooth and convex and the penalty is convex and separable by coordinate, so exact one-dimensional minimisation steps decrease the objective and reach the global minimum.

constraints: α — overall penalty strength, chosen by cross-validation along a path
l1_ratio ρ in [0, 1] — mix between L1 (sparse) and L2 (grouping)
tol and max iterations — stopping rule for the sweeps
Standardisation — features must be on the same scale for the penalty to be fair
edgeCases: Unscaled features are penalised unequally; standardise first
Intercept is not penalised, so centre y and X or fit it separately (this code has no intercept)
Convergence is slow for highly correlated features and small α
Selected features can change across resamples; check stability, not just one fit

problems.title: Entropy, Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence
problems.summary: Entropy measures the uncertainty of a distribution, cross-entropy the cost of describing it with another one, and KL divergence the extra cost.
problems.bruteForce: KL is asymmetric and infinite when q is zero where p is not, so for a symmetric bounded measure use Jensen-Shannon or a Wasserstein distance.
problems.intuition: Entropy is the average surprise of samples from p when you code them optimally. Cross-entropy H(p, q) is the average surprise if you use q's code instead, and the gap between the two is KL, a one-sided measure of how badly q approximates p. Because H(p) is fixed by the data, minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising KL.
problems.whyItWorks: KL is non-negative by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave log, and is zero only when q equals p almost everywhere. That makes cross-entropy minimised exactly when the model matches the data distribution, which is why it is the standard classification loss.
approach: Drop zero-probability terms of p — 0·log 0 is defined as 0
Entropy is the negative sum of p·log p — average surprise under p
Cross-entropy swaps in log q — cost of coding p's samples with q
KL is cross-entropy minus entropy — the pure mismatch term
Use natural log for nats, log base 2 for bits — only changes the scale
problems.time: O(k) for k outcomes
problems.space: O(k)
dryRun: H(p) = −Σ p(x) log p(x)
H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log q(x)
KL(p ‖ q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x) / q(x))
KL(p ‖ q) = H(p, q) − H(p)
KL(p ‖ q) ≥ 0, equality iff p = q
KL(p ‖ q) ≠ KL(q ‖ p) in general
problems.description: Training and evaluating classifiers, comparing distributions, VAEs, distillation, and anywhere you need a divergence between probabilities.

examples.input: Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?
examples.output: With one-hot labels it is the negative log-likelihood of the true class, and its minimiser makes the model distribution match the data distribution.

examples.input: What is the difference between forward and reverse KL?
examples.output: Forward KL(p‖q) is mass-covering, so q spreads over all modes of p; reverse KL(q‖p) is mode-seeking, so q locks onto one mode.

examples.input: Is KL divergence a distance?
examples.output: No. It is asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

constraints: Log base (natural log for nats, base 2 for bits)
Direction of the KL (forward KL(p‖q) or reverse KL(q‖p))
Smoothing epsilon added to q to avoid log of zero
edgeCases: KL is not symmetric and is not a true distance
q must be positive wherever p is, otherwise KL is infinite
Framework kl_div functions expect log-probabilities as input and probabilities as target
Inputs must be normalised distributions

problems.title: Exponential Smoothing (Simple and Holt)
problems.summary: Forecast a series with a running level (and optionally a trend) that is nudged toward each new observation by a smoothing weight. Simple smoothing gives a flat forecast; Holt's method adds a linear trend.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the series has seasonality you have not modelled (use Holt-Winters), when you need prediction intervals from a fitted likelihood, or when external regressors drive the series.
problems.intuition: The newest observation is the best clue about where the series is now, but a single value is noisy. Blending it with the previous estimate gives weights on past values that decay geometrically, so recent data matters most and old data fades without being stored.
problems.whyItWorks: Unrolling the recursion ℓ = α y + (1 − α) ℓ shows the level is a weighted average of all past observations with weights α(1 − α)ᵏ that sum to one. It is the optimal one-step predictor for a random walk plus noise, and Holt's method is the same idea applied to level and slope.
approach: Choose a start level ℓ₀ (and slope b₀ for Holt) — the recursion needs a state before the first observation
For each point, record the one-step prediction from the current state — these are the fitted values used to score the model
Update the level as a blend of the observation and the predicted level — α sets how fast old data is forgotten
For Holt, update the slope from the change in level — β sets how quickly the trend can change
Forecast ahead from the final state, flat for simple and linear for Holt — no further data is available to update it
problems.time: O(n) per pass; fitting α and β with a numerical optimiser multiplies this by the number of evaluations
problems.space: O(1) state for forecasting, O(n) if the fitted values are stored
dryRun: Simple: ℓₜ = α yₜ + (1 − α) ℓₜ₋₁,  ŷₜ₊₁|ₜ = ℓₜ
Unrolled: ℓₜ = Σₖ α(1−α)ᵏ yₜ₋ₖ + (1−α)ᵗ ℓ₀
Holt level: ℓₜ = α yₜ + (1 − α)(ℓₜ₋₁ + bₜ₋₁)
Holt trend: bₜ = β (ℓₜ − ℓₜ₋₁) + (1 − β) bₜ₋₁
Forecast: ŷₜ₊ₕ|ₜ = ℓₜ + h bₜ
Fit: minimise Σₜ (yₜ − ŷₜ|ₜ₋₁)² over α, β (and ℓ₀, b₀)
problems.description: Short-horizon forecasts of many series, a cheap and strong baseline, demand or traffic with slowly drifting level, and online updating where only the last state is kept.

examples.input: Why is it called exponential smoothing?
examples.output: Unrolling the recursion gives each past observation a weight that shrinks by a constant factor (1 − α) per step back, an exponential decay that sums to one.

examples.input: What do α near 0 and α near 1 mean?
examples.output: α near 1 trusts the latest value and nearly copies it forward, a naive forecast; α near 0 keeps the initial level almost unchanged, close to a long-run average.

examples.input: Why does simple smoothing fail on trending data?
examples.output: Its forecast is a weighted average of past values, so it always lags behind a rising or falling series; Holt's slope term removes that lag.

constraints: α level smoothing in (0, 1) — large reacts fast, small averages more
β trend smoothing in (0, 1) — large lets the slope change quickly
Initial level and slope — first value or a regression on the first few points
Damping φ — optional factor that flattens a Holt trend over long horizons (not in this code)
edgeCases: Undamped Holt trends extrapolate forever and overshoot at long horizons
A high α on a noisy series chases noise; the fitted values lag turning points when α is small
The start state matters for short series, so conventions differ between libraries
Pick α and β by one-step error on held-out data, not by eye

problems.title: Feature Scaling
problems.summary: Rescale each feature to a comparable range so distance-based and gradient-based models are not dominated by whichever feature has the largest units. Standard, min-max and robust scalers differ in what they subtract and divide by.
problems.bruteForce: Tree-based models (splits are invariant to monotone rescaling) and features already on a meaningful common scale. Do not fit the scaler on test data.
problems.intuition: Many models implicitly compare features with one shared yardstick: distances add squared differences, and a single learning rate steps every weight. A feature measured in thousands then drowns one measured in fractions. Scaling gives every feature the same units of spread, and the choice of centre and spread decides how outliers behave.
problems.whyItWorks: Each scaler is an affine map z = (x − c) / s with a per-feature centre and scale. Standardisation uses mean and standard deviation, min-max uses the minimum and range, and the robust scaler uses median and interquartile range, which a few extreme values barely move. Affine maps keep order and shape, so only the geometry the model sees changes.
approach: Choose centre and scale statistics per feature — they define the scaler
Compute them on the training rows only — held-out rows must not influence them
Replace zero scales with 1 — a constant column would divide by zero
Apply (x − centre) / scale to train, validation and test — same parameters everywhere
Invert with x = z·scale + centre when you need original units — the map is affine
problems.time: O(n·d) to fit and to apply (percentiles need a partial sort)
problems.space: O(d) for the stored centre and scale
dryRun: Standard: z = (x − μ) / σ
Min-max: z = (x − min) / (max − min)
Robust: z = (x − median) / (Q3 − Q1)
Fit statistics on train only, then apply to val/test
Constant column: scale 0 is replaced by 1, so z = 0
problems.description: k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, regularised linear models and neural networks, and anything optimised with gradient descent.

examples.input: Which models need feature scaling?
examples.output: Distance-based (k-NN, k-means, SVM), regularised and gradient-trained models; trees do not, since splits depend only on feature order.

examples.input: Standardisation or min-max?
examples.output: Standardise by default; use min-max when a bounded range is required and outliers are absent, and robust scaling when outliers are present.

examples.input: How does scaling relate to data leakage?
examples.output: The scaler's statistics are learned parameters, so fit them on training data only; fitting on everything lets test rows shape the transform.

constraints: Which scaler — standard, min-max or robust
Quantile range for the robust scaler
Output range for min-max, such as 0 to 1 or −1 to 1
edgeCases: Fitting on all data before splitting leaks test statistics
Min-max is dominated by a single outlier, squeezing everything else
Test values outside the train range land outside the target range
Scaling a one-hot or sparse matrix by its mean destroys sparsity

problems.title: Focal Loss
problems.summary: Cross-entropy multiplied by (1 − pₜ)^γ, which down-weights examples the model already classifies confidently so training focuses on hard ones.
problems.bruteForce: Balanced problems where plain cross-entropy works, or when labels are noisy: the loss up-weights hard examples, which may be the mislabelled ones. Probabilities from a focal-trained model are also usually less calibrated.
problems.intuition: With extreme imbalance, such as thousands of easy background boxes per object, the many easy examples each contribute a tiny loss but their sum swamps the few hard ones. The modulating factor (1 − pₜ)^γ is near zero when the model is right and confident, and near one when it is wrong, so easy examples fade out of the gradient. Setting γ to zero recovers ordinary weighted cross-entropy.
problems.whyItWorks: The factor reshapes the per-example loss so confident-correct examples contribute far less, while misclassified ones keep nearly their full cross-entropy. The total gradient is then dominated by informative hard examples instead of the large pool of easy negatives. The α weight separately balances positive and negative classes.
approach: Compute log pₜ stably from the logit with logaddexp — avoids log of zero for confident predictions
Get pₜ by exponentiating — the probability of the true class
Compute the class weight αₜ — balances positives against negatives
Multiply cross-entropy by αₜ·(1 − pₜ)^γ and average — easy examples contribute almost nothing
problems.time: O(N) for N logits
problems.space: O(N) for intermediates
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def focal_loss(z, y, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25):
    s = 2 * y - 1
    logpt = -np.logaddexp(0, -s * z)
    pt = np.exp(logpt)
    at = alpha * y + (1 - alpha) * (1 - y)
    return -(at * (1 - pt) ** gamma * logpt).mean()

def focal_grad(z, y, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25):
    s = 2 * y - 1
    logpt = -np.logaddexp(0, -s * z)
    pt = np.exp(logpt)
    at = alpha * y + (1 - alpha) * (1 - y)
    g = s * at * (1 - pt) ** gamma
    return g * (gamma * pt * logpt - (1 - pt)) / z.size
dryRun: p = σ(z),  pₜ = p if y = 1 else 1 − p
αₜ = α if y = 1 else 1 − α
FL = − αₜ · (1 − pₜ)^γ · log pₜ
With γ = 0 and α = 0.5: half of binary cross-entropy
∂FL/∂z = s·αₜ·(1−pₜ)^γ·[γ·pₜ·log pₜ − (1−pₜ)],  s = 2y − 1
problems.description: Dense detectors (RetinaNet) and other classification problems with heavy class imbalance and many easy negatives.

examples.input: What does the (1 − pₜ)^γ factor do?
examples.output: It shrinks the loss of well-classified examples, so the few hard examples dominate training.

examples.input: How does focal loss differ from class weighting?
examples.output: Class weights rebalance by class, while the focal factor rebalances by difficulty, regardless of class.

examples.input: What happens when γ = 0?
examples.output: It reduces to α-weighted cross-entropy.

constraints: Focusing parameter γ
Class weight α
Reduction (mean here; sum or per-anchor normalisation in detectors)
edgeCases: Binary (sigmoid) form only; the multi-class softmax form is not covered here
α and γ interact, so tune them together
Initialise the final bias for the rare class's prior or training can be unstable at the start
Detectors normalise by the number of positive anchors; this sketch uses a plain mean

problems.title: Generalised Advantage Estimation
problems.summary: Estimate how much better an action was than average by summing one-step temporal-difference errors with exponentially decaying weights, trading bias against variance with a single parameter λ.
problems.bruteForce: When no value function is learned (pure REINFORCE with a baseline from returns), or when the critic is so poor that bootstrapping hurts. Off-policy replay needs importance-corrected estimators instead.
problems.intuition: A one-step estimate of an action's advantage trusts the value function heavily: low variance but biased if the critic is wrong. A full Monte-Carlo return trusts only observed rewards: unbiased but noisy. GAE blends them: each TD error δ looks one step ahead, and the advantage is a decayed sum of future TD errors, with γλ controlling how far the sum reaches. Computing it is a simple backward recursion over the trajectory.
problems.whyItWorks: The sum of TD errors with weights (γλ)^l is an exponentially weighted average of n-step advantage estimates. λ = 0 recovers the one-step TD error and λ = 1 recovers the Monte-Carlo advantage, with intermediate values interpolating. Because the weights decay geometrically, the whole sum satisfies A_t = δ_t + γλ·A_{t+1}, so a single backward pass computes every advantage in linear time.
approach: Compute the TD error δ_t for every step, bootstrapping from V(s_{t+1}) unless the episode ended — the one-step advantage signal
Start at the end of the rollout with a running advantage of zero — nothing lies beyond the horizon
Walk backwards: add δ_t to γλ times the next step's advantage — accumulates decayed future TD errors
Reset the running sum across episode boundaries using the done flag — advantages must not leak between episodes
Return advantages and A + V as value targets — the policy and critic training signals
problems.time: O(T) for a rollout of T steps
problems.space: O(T) for the TD errors and advantages
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def gae(rewards, values, last_value, dones, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    # dones[t] = 1 if the episode ended after step t
    v_next = np.append(values[1:], last_value)
    alive = 1.0 - dones
    delta = rewards + gamma * alive * v_next - values
    adv = np.zeros(len(rewards))
    run = 0.0
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):
        run = delta[t] + gamma * lam * alive[t] * run
        adv[t] = run
    return adv, adv + values      # advantages, value targets
dryRun: TD error: δ_t = r_t + γ·(1 − d_t)·V(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t)
GAE: A_t = Σ_{l≥0} (γλ)^l · δ_{t+l}   (stops at episode end)
Recursion: A_t = δ_t + γλ·(1 − d_t)·A_{t+1}
λ = 0:  A_t = δ_t   (one-step TD)
λ = 1:  A_t = G_t − V(s_t)   (Monte-Carlo advantage)
Value target: A_t + V(s_t)
d_t = 1 if the episode ends after step t, else 0
problems.description: Actor-critic methods such as PPO and A2C, where a value function is available and advantages should be less noisy than raw returns.

examples.input: What do λ = 0 and λ = 1 give?
examples.output: λ = 0 gives the one-step TD error, low variance but biased by the critic. λ = 1 gives the discounted Monte-Carlo return minus the value baseline, unbiased but high variance.

examples.input: Why is GAE computed backwards?
examples.output: Each advantage equals its own TD error plus γλ times the next advantage, so iterating from the end reuses the already-computed suffix and costs linear time.

examples.input: What does the done flag do in the recursion?
examples.output: It removes the bootstrap term at a terminal state and stops the running sum from carrying future advantages across an episode boundary.

constraints: Discount γ
GAE parameter λ (low is biased and low variance, high is unbiased and noisy)
Rollout length (sets how far bootstrapping from last_value reaches)
Advantage normalisation across the batch
edgeCases: Bootstrap from last_value only if the rollout was cut off; a terminated episode must have done = 1 at its final step
Time-limit truncation is not a true terminal and should still bootstrap from the value of the final state; this code treats done as terminal
Values and last_value come from the critic at collection time and are not differentiated through
This handles one environment; vectorised rollouts apply the same recursion per environment

problems.title: GAN Minimax Loss (Saturating vs Non-Saturating)
problems.summary: A discriminator learns to tell real data from generated data with a binary cross-entropy loss, while the generator is trained to make the discriminator fail, either by minimising log(1 − D(G(z))) or by maximising log D(G(z)).
problems.bruteForce: When you need stable training or a likelihood: GAN training is notoriously unstable and prone to mode collapse. Diffusion models or VAEs are often easier to train.
problems.intuition: The generator is trained only through the discriminator's verdict on its samples. Early in training the discriminator easily rejects fakes, and the original saturating loss then has almost no gradient exactly when the generator most needs a signal. Flipping the target to maximise log D(G(z)) has the same fixed point but a strong gradient when the discriminator is winning.
problems.whyItWorks: For a fixed generator the best discriminator is the density ratio of real to total, and plugging it in turns the game into a Jensen-Shannon divergence between real and generated distributions, minimised when they match. The non-saturating loss has the same fixed point but, as the logit of a fake goes very negative, its gradient stays near constant while the saturating gradient shrinks to zero. This code scores logits only; it does not model D or G networks.
approach: Let D output a logit and treat σ(logit) as P(real) — keeps the loss stable in logit space
D loss is softplus(−logit on real) + softplus(logit on fake) — binary cross-entropy with labels 1 and 0
Saturating G loss is the negative of the fake term — the minimax game, G minimises log(1 − D(G(z)))
Non-saturating G loss is softplus(−logit on fake) — cross-entropy with the fake labelled real
Compare gradients with respect to the fake logit — the saturating one vanishes when D is confident
problems.time: O(n) for n logits, plus the cost of running G and D
problems.space: O(n)
dryRun: D(x) = σ(ℓ(x)),  ℓ = discriminator logit
L_D = −E[log D(x)] − E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]
L_G^sat = E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]   (G minimises)
L_G^ns = −E[log D(G(z))]
−log σ(ℓ) = softplus(−ℓ),  −log(1 − σ(ℓ)) = softplus(ℓ)
∂L_G^sat/∂ℓ_f = −σ(ℓ_f)/n,   ∂L_G^ns/∂ℓ_f = (σ(ℓ_f) − 1)/n
Optimal D* = p_data / (p_data + p_g)
problems.description: Understanding and implementing adversarial training for image and other generators, and as the starting point for variants such as Wasserstein and hinge-loss GANs.

examples.input: Why is the original generator loss called saturating?
examples.output: When D confidently rejects a fake, D(G(z)) is near 0 and log(1 − D) is flat there, so the gradient to G is almost zero when G is worst.

examples.input: Does the non-saturating loss change the equilibrium?
examples.output: No, both are minimised when the generated distribution equals the data. Only the gradient strength away from equilibrium differs; it is a heuristic, not the exact minimax game.

examples.input: What is mode collapse?
examples.output: The generator maps many inputs to a few outputs that fool D, so it covers only part of the data distribution.

constraints: Ratio of discriminator to generator updates
Learning rates and Adam β₁ for each network
Latent noise dimension
Loss variant (saturating, non-saturating, hinge, Wasserstein)
edgeCases: Computing log(sigmoid) directly overflows; use softplus on logits as here
D should be updated with fake samples detached from G's graph
A very strong D starves G of gradient; balance the two networks

problems.title: Gaussian Mixture Model (EM)
problems.summary: Model the data as a weighted sum of Gaussians and fit it by alternating soft cluster assignments (E-step) with weighted parameter updates (M-step). It is k-means with soft membership and per-cluster covariance.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it for non-convex shapes (use DBSCAN or spectral clustering), when clusters are tiny relative to the dimension (covariances become singular), or when you need a unique answer independent of initialisation.
problems.intuition: If you knew which Gaussian produced each point, fitting would be trivial weighted averaging; if you knew the Gaussians, assigning points would be trivial Bayes' rule. EM breaks the chicken-and-egg loop by using the current guess to assign fractional responsibilities, refitting with them, and repeating, and each round can never lower the likelihood.
problems.whyItWorks: The log-likelihood has a sum inside the log, so it has no closed form. EM maximises a lower bound that is tight at the current parameters (Jensen's inequality): the E-step makes the bound touch the likelihood, and the M-step raises the bound, so the likelihood is non-decreasing. It converges to a local optimum, not necessarily the global one.
approach: Initialise means, equal weights and the data covariance — any start works but the result depends on it
Compute log πₖ N(x; μₖ, Σₖ) per point and component with a Cholesky solve — stable and gives the log-determinant for free
Normalise with log-sum-exp to get responsibilities — turns joint densities into soft assignments without underflow
Re-estimate weights, means and covariances weighted by responsibilities — the exact maximiser given the soft labels
Add a small ε to each covariance diagonal — stops a component collapsing onto one point
Stop when the log-likelihood gain is tiny — it never decreases, so the gain is a safe test
problems.time: O(iters·n·K·d²) plus O(K·d³) per iteration for the Cholesky factors
problems.space: O(n·K) for responsibilities, O(K·d²) for covariances
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def log_joint(X, w, mu, S):
    out = []
    for k in range(len(w)):
        L = np.linalg.cholesky(S[k])
        z = np.linalg.solve(L, (X - mu[k]).T)
        ld = 2 * np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
        q = (z ** 2).sum(0) + ld + X.shape[1] * np.log(2 * np.pi)
        out.append(np.log(w[k]) - 0.5 * q)
    return np.stack(out, 1)

def em(X, mu, iters=200, reg=1e-6):
    n, d = X.shape
    K = len(mu)
    w = np.full(K, 1 / K)
    S = np.array([np.cov(X.T, bias=True) + reg * np.eye(d)] * K)
    ll = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        lj = log_joint(X, w, mu, S)
        m = lj.max(1, keepdims=True)
        tot = m + np.log(np.exp(lj - m).sum(1, keepdims=True))
        R = np.exp(lj - tot)
        ll.append(tot.sum())
        Nk = R.sum(0)
        w, mu = Nk / n, R.T @ X / Nk[:, None]
        for k in range(K):
            D = X - mu[k]
            S[k] = (R[:, k] * D.T) @ D / Nk[k] + reg * np.eye(d)
        if len(ll) > 1 and ll[-1] - ll[-2] < 1e-10:
            break
    return w, mu, S, ll
dryRun: p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x; μₖ, Σₖ)
log N = −½ [ d·log 2π + log|Σ| + (x−μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x−μ) ]
E-step: rᵢₖ = πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ; μⱼ, Σⱼ)
Nₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ
M-step: πₖ = Nₖ / n,  μₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ xᵢ / Nₖ
Σₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ (xᵢ−μₖ)(xᵢ−μₖ)ᵀ / Nₖ + ε I
Objective: ℓ = Σᵢ log Σₖ πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ)
problems.description: Soft clustering with elliptical clusters of different size and shape, density estimation, anomaly scoring by low likelihood, and as a generative model per class.

examples.input: How is a GMM different from k-means?
examples.output: k-means is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-covariance limit of EM; a GMM gives soft responsibilities and learns each cluster's weight and covariance.

examples.input: Why does EM never decrease the likelihood?
examples.output: The E-step builds a lower bound equal to the likelihood at the current parameters and the M-step maximises that bound, so the true likelihood can only go up.

examples.input: How do you pick the number of components?
examples.output: Fit several K and compare BIC, which penalises parameters, or compare held-out log-likelihood; likelihood on training data always improves with K.

examples.input: What goes wrong when a covariance is singular?
examples.output: The density at that component's point blows up, so the fit chases a spike; a covariance floor or priors prevent it.

constraints: n_components K — choose by BIC/AIC or held-out likelihood
covariance_type — full, tied, diagonal or spherical (this code is full only)
reg_covar ε — floor added to covariance diagonals
Initialisation and n_init — several restarts guard against poor local optima
edgeCases: Local optima: different starts give different fits, so run several restarts
A component can collapse onto a single point, sending the likelihood to infinity without the ε floor
Component labels are arbitrary, so compare fits after matching components
Likelihood alone always favours more components; penalise with BIC or validate on held-out data

problems.title: Gaussian Process Regression
problems.summary: Place a Gaussian process prior over functions, condition it on noisy observations, and get a predictive mean and variance at any new input in closed form. The kernel decides what kind of functions are plausible.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it for large n, since training cubes and memory squares with the number of points, for high dimensional inputs with weak structure, or when a fast approximate model is enough.
problems.intuition: Instead of fitting parameters, keep every training point and let the kernel say how strongly nearby inputs share their outputs. Close to data the prediction is pinned down and the variance is small; far from data it falls back to the prior mean with the prior variance, so the model knows what it does not know.
problems.whyItWorks: Any finite set of function values under the prior is a multivariate Gaussian, and a joint Gaussian conditioned on some coordinates is again Gaussian with a mean and covariance given by linear algebra. The posterior mean is a kernel-weighted sum of the training targets, the same form as kernel ridge regression with the noise as the ridge.
approach: Build the kernel matrix on the training inputs and add the noise variance to its diagonal — noise makes it positive definite and stops exact interpolation
Factor it with a Cholesky decomposition — cheaper and more stable than inverting
Solve for α = K⁻¹y with two triangular solves — the prediction weights on the training targets
Compute the cross kernel between test and train points and form the mean as a weighted sum — predictions
Solve L v = k* and subtract vᵀv from the prior variance — uncertainty shrinks where data is nearby
Evaluate the log marginal likelihood from the same factor — the score used to tune ℓ, s² and noise
problems.time: O(n³) for the Cholesky factor, O(n·m) per extra test point for the mean and O(n²·m) for variances
problems.space: O(n²) for the kernel matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def rbf(A, B, ell, s2):
    d2 = ((A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
    return s2 * np.exp(-d2 / (2 * ell ** 2))

def gp(X, y, Xs, ell, s2, noise):
    K = rbf(X, X, ell, s2) + noise * np.eye(len(X))
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)
    a = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, y))
    Ks = rbf(X, Xs, ell, s2)
    v = np.linalg.solve(L, Ks)
    mean = Ks.T @ a
    var = s2 - (v ** 2).sum(0)
    lml = (-0.5 * y @ a - np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
           - 0.5 * len(X) * np.log(2 * np.pi))
    return mean, var, lml
dryRun: Prior: f ~ GP(0, k),  k(x, x′) = s² exp(−‖x − x′‖² / 2ℓ²)
Noisy targets: y = f(x) + ε,  ε ~ N(0, σₙ²)
K = k(X, X) + σₙ² I,  K = L Lᵀ (Cholesky)
α = K⁻¹ y = Lᵀ \ (L \ y)
Mean: μ* = k(X*, X) α
Variance of f: σ*² = k(x*, x*) − ‖L⁻¹ k(X, x*)‖²
log p(y) = −½ yᵀα − Σᵢ log Lᵢᵢ − (n/2) log 2π
problems.description: Small or medium datasets where calibrated uncertainty matters, Bayesian optimisation surrogates, smooth interpolation of expensive simulations, and regression where a kernel encodes domain knowledge.

examples.input: How is a GP different from kernel ridge regression?
examples.output: The posterior mean has the same form as kernel ridge with the noise variance as the ridge, but a GP also returns a predictive variance and tunes the kernel by marginal likelihood.

examples.input: What does the length scale control?
examples.output: How quickly the function varies: a short length scale gives wiggly fits that revert to the prior quickly, a long one gives smooth, slowly varying fits.

examples.input: Why use a Cholesky factor instead of a matrix inverse?
examples.output: It is faster and numerically stable for symmetric positive definite matrices and gives the log-determinant needed for the marginal likelihood for free.

constraints: Length scale ℓ — how far apart inputs can be and still be correlated
Signal variance s² — prior amplitude of the function
Noise variance σₙ² — observation noise, also acts as a jitter for stability
Kernel family — RBF, Matérn, periodic, or sums and products of them
Optimiser restarts — the marginal likelihood is non-convex in the hyperparameters
edgeCases: Training cost grows as n cubed, so thousands of points need sparse or inducing-point approximations
Tiny noise makes the kernel matrix near singular and the Cholesky fail; add jitter
The variance returned here is for the latent function; add the noise variance for a new observation
A zero prior mean pulls predictions to zero away from data; centre or normalise the targets

problems.title: GNN Message Passing (GCN Layer)
problems.summary: Update each node by averaging its own and its neighbours' features with symmetric degree normalisation, then applying a shared linear map and nonlinearity.
problems.bruteForce: Very deep stacks, because repeated averaging over-smooths node features until they look alike, or tasks needing edge features or anisotropic neighbour weights, where GAT or message-passing variants fit better.
problems.intuition: A node cannot see the whole graph, so it learns from its neighbourhood: each layer collects messages from adjacent nodes and mixes them with its own state. Stacking k layers lets information travel k hops. The normalisation by degrees stops high-degree nodes from dominating, and the added self-loop keeps a node's own features in the mix.
problems.whyItWorks: Each layer is a first-order approximation of a spectral graph filter, so it low-pass filters node signals over the graph, which suits tasks where connected nodes tend to share labels. Symmetric normalisation keeps the eigenvalues of the propagation matrix in a stable range, so repeated application does not blow up or collapse the scale.
approach: Add self-loops, Â = A + I — each node keeps its own features in the sum
Compute degrees d̃ of Â — needed for normalisation
Scale to Â_norm = D̃^(−1/2) Â D̃^(−1/2) — symmetric weights stop hubs from blowing up the scale
Aggregate neighbour features with Â_norm X — the message-passing step
Apply the shared weight W and ReLU — transforms the aggregated features like a dense layer
problems.time: O(N²·F + N·F·F') dense; O(E·F + N·F·F') with sparse edges
problems.space: O(N²) dense adjacency; O(E) sparse
dryRun: Â = A + I,   D̃ᵢᵢ = Σⱼ Âᵢⱼ
Per node: hᵢ' = σ( Σⱼ∈N(i)∪{i} (1/√(d̃ᵢ d̃ⱼ)) · W hⱼ )
H ∈ ℝ^(N×F), W ∈ ℝ^(F×F'), A ∈ {0,1}^(N×N) symmetric
k layers aggregate information from k-hop neighbourhoods
problems.description: Node classification and link prediction on citation, social or molecular graphs where neighbours carry signal, and with moderate graph sizes.

examples.input: Why add self-loops?
examples.output: Without Â = A + I a node would ignore its own features after aggregation and nodes with no neighbours would receive nothing.

examples.input: Why symmetric normalisation instead of dividing by degree?
examples.output: D^(−1/2) A D^(−1/2) treats both endpoints' degrees, keeping the operator symmetric with stable eigenvalues, while row normalisation only averages.

examples.input: What is over-smoothing?
examples.output: Repeated neighbourhood averaging pushes node representations toward each other, so deep GCNs lose the ability to tell nodes apart.

examples.input: What is the receptive field after k layers?
examples.output: Nodes within k hops of the target.

constraints: Number of layers (hops)
Hidden width F'
Dropout rate on features and edges
Normalisation scheme (symmetric, row, none)
edgeCases: Assumes an undirected graph with a symmetric 0/1 adjacency; directed graphs need care
A dense N×N adjacency does not scale; real code uses sparse edge lists
Stacking many layers over-smooths
No bias, dropout or edge weights in this sketch

problems.title: Gradient Boosting
problems.summary: Build a model as a sum of many weak trees, each fitted to the errors the current sum still makes. The code is simplified to squared loss with depth-1 trees (stumps), which is exactly what sklearn does for that setting.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when training must be parallel or tiny, with very noisy labels (it keeps fitting noise without early stopping), or when you need extrapolation.
problems.intuition: Instead of one big model, keep a running prediction and repeatedly ask "what is still wrong?". For squared loss the answer is just the residuals, so each new small tree learns to correct the leftover error, and a small learning rate makes each correction cautious.
problems.whyItWorks: Boosting is gradient descent in function space. The residual y − F(x) is the negative gradient of the squared loss with respect to the prediction, so fitting a tree to it moves F downhill on the loss. Swap the loss and the same loop gives classification or robust regression by fitting the new negative gradients instead.
approach: Start from the mean of y — the best constant prediction
Compute residuals y − F — they are the negative gradient of the loss
Find the stump that best fits the residuals — sorted cumulative sums score every split at once
Add η times the stump to F — a small step avoids overfitting
Repeat for M rounds — each round removes more of the remaining error
problems.time: O(M · d · n log n) with a sort per feature per round; prediction is O(M)
problems.space: O(M) for the stumps plus O(n) for the running prediction
dryRun: F₀(x) = ȳ  (best constant for squared loss)
rᵢ = yᵢ − Fₘ₋₁(xᵢ) = −∂L/∂F  for L = ½(y − F)²
hₘ = tree fitted to the residuals r
Fₘ(x) = Fₘ₋₁(x) + η · hₘ(x)
Stump: h(x) = a if xⱼ ≤ t else b
a, b = mean residual on each side of the split
Best split maximises (Σ_L r)²/|L| + (Σ_R r)²/|R|
problems.description: Usually the most accurate choice on tabular data, for both regression and classification, when you can afford some tuning.

examples.input: Why is it called gradient boosting?
examples.output: Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction, so adding it is a gradient descent step in function space.

examples.input: Bagging vs boosting?
examples.output: Bagging averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees sequentially to cut bias.

examples.input: What is the trade-off between learning rate and number of trees?
examples.output: A smaller rate needs more trees but usually gives better generalisation; tune them together with early stopping.

constraints: n_estimators M — more rounds fit more; use early stopping
learning_rate η — smaller needs more rounds but generalises better
max_depth — depth 1 gives additive models, 3-6 allows interactions
subsample — fraction of rows per round (stochastic boosting)
loss — squared, absolute, Huber, or log-loss for classification
