examples.output: After the addition, so the block output is non-negative; pre-activation variants move BN and ReLU before each conv instead.

examples.input: Why no bias in the convolutions?
examples.output: The following batch norm has its own shift β, which makes a conv bias redundant.

constraints: Channels per stage and number of blocks per stage
Stride of the first block in each stage (downsampling)
BatchNorm ε and momentum
Zero-initialising the last BN γ so each block starts as identity
edgeCases: This code uses batch statistics only (train mode); inference needs running averages
Adding before the ReLU versus after changes the function; follow the variant you load weights for
A stride-2 first conv with an identity shortcut fails on shape; use the projection
Loops make this very slow; it is for understanding, not training

problems.title: Retrieval Metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG)
problems.summary: Judge a ranked list of documents against known relevance labels: did the relevant ones appear in the top k, how high was the first one, and how good is the whole ordering.
problems.bruteForce: When no relevance judgements are available, or when answer quality rather than retrieval quality is the goal; a high Recall@k does not guarantee a good generated answer. MRR ignores everything after the first relevant hit.
problems.intuition: A retriever returns an ordered list, so correctness depends on position as well as membership. Recall@k asks what fraction of the relevant items made the top k, MRR rewards putting the first relevant item high, and nDCG discounts each item's relevance by the log of its rank and divides by the best possible ordering, so a perfect ranking scores one and graded relevance is handled.
problems.whyItWorks: Users only look at the top of a list, so metrics weight early ranks more. Recall@k suits a first-stage retriever that feeds a reranker or a language model, because only missing a relevant item is unrecoverable. The logarithmic discount in DCG decays smoothly, and normalising by the ideal DCG makes scores comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.
approach: Rank documents for each query by score, highest first — the ordering is what is being judged
Look up each ranked document's relevance label — turns scores into a sequence of hits and misses
Recall@k: relevant hits in the first k divided by all relevant — did the retriever find them
MRR: reciprocal of the rank of the first hit — how soon does the user see something useful
nDCG@k: discounted gain divided by the ideal discounted gain — position-aware and normalised to one
problems.time: O(Q·D log D) to sort D documents for each of Q queries
problems.space: O(Q·D) for the score and label matrices
dryRun: Recall@k = |relevant ∩ top-k| / |relevant|
RR = 1 / rank of first relevant item;  MRR = mean of RR over queries
DCG@k = Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ relᵢ / log₂(i + 1)    (linear gain)
nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k
IDCG@k: DCG@k of the ideal ordering (labels sorted descending)
Each metric is averaged over queries
problems.description: Evaluating search, recommender candidate generation and the retrieval step of RAG systems when relevance labels exist for each query.

examples.input: When is Recall@k the right metric for retrieval?
examples.output: For a first-stage retriever feeding a reranker or an LLM, since anything missing from the top k can never be recovered later. Order within the top k matters less.

examples.input: Why does nDCG normalise by the ideal DCG?
examples.output: Raw DCG grows with the number of relevant items, so queries are not comparable. Dividing by the best achievable DCG puts every query on a zero-to-one scale.

examples.input: How do MRR and nDCG differ?
examples.output: MRR only looks at the first relevant item and treats relevance as binary. nDCG uses the whole ranked list and supports graded relevance with a smooth position discount.

constraints: Cut-off k (match the number of items a downstream stage or user actually sees)
Gain function (linear relevance here; 2^rel − 1 is also common)
Relevance grades (binary or graded)
Tie handling for equal scores
edgeCases: Queries with no relevant document divide by zero here; drop them or define them as zero
Gain choice matters: this code uses linear gain, which is what scikit-learn uses; other libraries use 2^rel − 1
Ties in scores are broken arbitrarily here by sort order; scikit-learn averages over ties by default
The nDCG code needs k no larger than the number of documents per query

problems.title: Reward Model (Bradley-Terry Loss)
problems.summary: Learn a scalar reward for text from human comparisons by training so that the preferred response scores higher than the rejected one, using a logistic loss on the score difference.
problems.bruteForce: When labels are absolute scores (use regression), when preferences are intransitive or inconsistent across annotators, or when the reward will be optimised so hard that the model exploits its errors.
problems.intuition: People find it easier to say which of two answers is better than to give an absolute score. The Bradley-Terry model turns that into probability: the chance that the chosen response wins is a sigmoid of the difference between the two rewards. Only the difference matters, so the learned rewards have no absolute scale or zero point, and the loss simply pushes the gap in the right direction with more force when the model currently has the pair the wrong way round.
problems.whyItWorks: Minimising the loss is maximum likelihood for the Bradley-Terry model, and the logistic loss is smooth and convex in a linear reward. The gradient on each pair is proportional to the probability the model assigns to the wrong ordering, so confident mistakes are corrected hardest while correctly ranked pairs fade out of the update.
approach: Score the chosen and rejected response with the reward model — a scalar for each
Take the difference d = r_c − r_r — Bradley-Terry only depends on the gap
Apply −log σ(d), computed as log(1 + e^(−d)) — negative log-likelihood that the chosen response wins
Average over pairs — one training objective for the batch
Step the reward model's parameters down the gradient — larger corrections for pairs currently ranked wrongly
problems.time: O(N·d) per pass for N pairs of d-dimensional features (a real reward model costs a transformer forward pass per response)
problems.space: O(N·d) for the pair features
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def bt_loss(w, Xc, Xr):
    # Xc, Xr: features of chosen / rejected responses (N x d)
    diff = Xc - Xr
    d = diff @ w                       # r_chosen - r_rejected
    loss = np.logaddexp(0.0, -d).mean()
    p = np.exp(-np.logaddexp(0.0, d))  # sigma(-d): P(wrong order)
    grad = -(diff.T @ p) / len(d)
    return loss, grad
dryRun: P(chosen ≻ rejected) = σ(r_c − r_r) = e^{r_c} / (e^{r_c} + e^{r_r})
Linear reward: r(x) = w·x
d = r_c − r_r = w·(x_c − x_r)
L = −mean log σ(d) = mean log(1 + e^(−d))
∂L/∂w = −mean[ σ(−d) · (x_c − x_r) ]
Shift invariance: adding any constant to both rewards leaves L fixed
problems.description: Building the reward model in RLHF from pairwise human or AI preference labels, or for any ranking problem trained on pairs.

examples.input: Why is the loss a function of the reward difference only?
examples.output: The Bradley-Terry probability that one item beats another is a sigmoid of the difference of their scores. Adding a constant to all scores cancels, so absolute reward values are unidentifiable.

examples.input: Why does the loss equal log(1 + e^(−d))?
examples.output: −log σ(d) = log(1 + e^(−d)). Computing it with logaddexp avoids overflow and underflow for large positive or negative differences.

examples.input: How does the reward model connect to DPO?
examples.output: DPO uses the same Bradley-Terry likelihood but defines the reward as a scaled log-ratio of policy to reference, so the policy itself plays the role of the reward model.

constraints: Learning rate and optimiser
Number of epochs (reward models overfit quickly on small preference sets)
L2 regularisation or reward centring
Base model and score head (here a linear head on fixed features)
edgeCases: Only reward differences are meaningful; normalise or centre rewards before using them elsewhere
This code uses a linear reward on fixed features; a real model scores text with a transformer and a scalar head on its final token
Noisy or contradictory labels cap how well pairs can be ordered
Policies optimised against the reward can exploit its mistakes (reward hacking)

problems.title: Ridge and Lasso Regularization
problems.summary: Add a penalty on the size of the weights to least squares. L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights smoothly and has a closed form; L1 (lasso) also sets some weights exactly to zero and is solved by coordinate descent.
problems.bruteForce: Skip them when features are few, independent and data plentiful (plain least squares is fine), or when lasso faces groups of correlated features (it picks one arbitrarily; try elastic net).
problems.intuition: Penalising weight size trades a little bias for a lot less variance, so the fit stops chasing noise or collinear directions. The L1 penalty has a sharp corner at zero, so small coefficients are pushed all the way to zero, while the smooth L2 penalty only shrinks them.
problems.whyItWorks: Ridge adds λI to XᵀX, which lifts every eigenvalue away from zero, so the system is always solvable and noisy low-variance directions are damped. For lasso, the one-coordinate subproblem has an exact soft-threshold solution: any coordinate whose correlation with the residual is below λ stays at zero.
approach: Centre X and y — so the intercept is not penalised
Ridge: solve (XᵀX + λI)w = Xᵀy — the added λI makes it well conditioned
Lasso: loop over coordinates, removing feature j from the residual — leaves the partial residual
Soft-threshold the correlation with that residual — this is the exact 1-D L1 minimiser
Put the coordinate back and repeat for several sweeps — convex, so it converges
Recover the intercept from the means — to predict on uncentred data
problems.time: Ridge O(n·d² + d³); lasso O(sweeps · n · d)
problems.space: O(d²) for ridge, O(n·d) for lasso
dryRun: Ridge: min ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖₂²
w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹ Xᵀy  (data centred, bias not penalised)
Lasso: min (1/2n)‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖₁
Soft(z, λ) = sign(z) · max(|z| − λ, 0)
wⱼ ← Soft(xⱼᵀr / n, λ) / (xⱼᵀxⱼ / n)
r = y − Σₖ≠ⱼ xₖwₖ  (partial residual)
Intercept b = ȳ − x̄ᵀw
problems.description: Many or correlated features, or fewer samples than features. Use ridge to stabilise and shrink, and lasso when you also want feature selection.

examples.input: Why does L1 give sparse weights and L2 does not?
examples.output: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero so the optimum often lands exactly on an axis; L2 has a smooth bowl whose gradient vanishes at zero, so weights shrink but rarely hit zero.

examples.input: What is the Bayesian view?
examples.output: Ridge is MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the weights; lasso is MAP with a Laplace prior.

examples.input: How do you choose λ?
examples.output: Cross-validate over a log-spaced grid and pick the value with the best validation error, or the largest one within one standard error of it.

constraints: λ (alpha) — penalty strength; choose by cross-validation
Penalty type — L2 (ridge), L1 (lasso), or a mix (elastic net)
Feature scaling — required, since the penalty depends on units
Sweeps / tolerance — stopping rule for lasso coordinate descent
edgeCases: Unscaled features are penalised unevenly, so standardise first
Do not penalise the intercept
Lasso picks one of several correlated features arbitrarily
sklearn's Ridge uses λ‖w‖² on the summed error but Lasso uses 1/(2n); the scales differ

problems.title: Adagrad and RMSProp
problems.summary: Give every parameter its own step size by dividing the gradient by the root of a running sum (Adagrad) or running average (RMSProp) of its squared past gradients.
problems.bruteForce: Adagrad on long non-convex training, where its steps decay too far. Neither is ideal when you need best final generalisation, where SGD with momentum often wins.
problems.intuition: Parameters with consistently large gradients get their step shrunk and rarely updated ones keep large steps, so one global learning rate no longer has to suit every direction. Adagrad sums squared gradients forever, so its steps only ever shrink and can stall. RMSProp swaps the sum for an exponential average, so old gradients are forgotten and the step size stays usable on long, non-convex runs.
problems.whyItWorks: Dividing by √v rescales each coordinate by its typical gradient size, acting like a diagonal preconditioner. Steep directions get smaller steps and flat directions larger ones, so progress is more even on badly scaled problems. The exponential average in RMSProp keeps the scale tied to recent gradients instead of the whole history.
approach: Keep one accumulator per parameter, started at zero — stores gradient scale history
Adagrad adds g² each step; RMSProp sets v = αv + (1 − α)g² — sum versus forgetting average
Take the square root of the accumulator and add ε — per-parameter scale, ε avoids dividing by zero
Divide the gradient by that scale — normalises the step so each coordinate moves a comparable amount
Scale by the learning rate and subtract from the weights — the actual update
problems.time: O(P) per step for P parameters
problems.space: O(P) for one extra accumulator
dryRun: Adagrad:  Gₜ = Gₜ₋₁ + gₜ²
wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η · gₜ / (√Gₜ + ε)
RMSProp:  vₜ = α vₜ₋₁ + (1 − α) gₜ²
wₜ₊₁ = wₜ − η · gₜ / (√vₜ + ε)
All operations are element-wise; ε is added outside the root
problems.description: Adagrad for sparse features (embeddings, bag-of-words) with convex-ish problems. RMSProp for non-stationary or non-convex training such as RNNs, and as the base of Adam.

examples.input: Why does Adagrad's learning rate decay?
examples.output: Its accumulator is a sum of squares that only grows, so the effective step η/√G keeps shrinking and training can stall.

examples.input: How does RMSProp fix that?
examples.output: It uses an exponential moving average of squared gradients, so old values fade and the scale tracks recent gradients.

examples.input: How does RMSProp relate to Adam?
examples.output: Adam is RMSProp-style scaling plus momentum on the gradient and bias correction of both averages.

examples.input: Where does ε go and why does it matter?
examples.output: PyTorch adds it after the square root, √v + ε; putting it inside the root, √(v + ε), is a different update, which matters when v is tiny.

constraints: Learning rate η
Decay rate α for RMSProp (commonly 0.9 to 0.99)
ε for numerical stability
Initial accumulator value (Adagrad)
edgeCases: The first RMSProp step is large because v starts at zero and is biased low
ε placement (inside versus outside the root) differs between libraries
Adagrad needs a larger learning rate than RMSProp because the accumulator grows
No momentum, weight decay or centring here; PyTorch offers them as options

problems.title: RNN Cell
problems.summary: Process a sequence one step at a time, mixing the current input with a hidden state that carries a summary of everything seen so far.
problems.bruteForce: Long-range dependencies, where gradients vanish or explode over many steps, and large-scale language tasks where attention-based models train in parallel and scale better.
problems.intuition: The hidden state is a small memory that is rewritten at every step: the new state is a squashed blend of the new input and the old state. The same weights are reused at every step, so the model handles any length with a fixed number of parameters, but information must survive being rewritten again and again.
problems.whyItWorks: The recurrence makes the final state a function of the whole input history, so a fixed-size network can read variable-length sequences. Weight sharing across time gives the same detector at every position. Training works through backpropagation through time, which multiplies many copies of the same Jacobian, and that repeated product is why gradients tend to vanish or explode.
approach: Compute x·Wxᵀ for the current input — projects the input into the hidden space
Compute h·Whᵀ for the previous state — lets the past influence the present
Add both and a bias, then apply tanh — keeps the state bounded and non-linear
Return the new state and feed it back in at the next step — this loop is the recurrence
Loop over the sequence with the same weights — parameter sharing across time
problems.time: O(T·H·(I+H)) for T steps, input size I and hidden size H
problems.space: O(T·H) to store all hidden states for backprop through time
dryRun: hₜ = tanh(Wₓxₜ + W_h hₜ₋₁ + b)
Wₓ: H × I,  W_h: H × H,  b: H
∂hₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ = diag(1 − hₜ²) W_h
∂h_T/∂h_k = Π over t = k+1..T of diag(1 − hₜ²) W_h
problems.description: Small sequence problems, teaching, and as the building block to understand LSTMs and GRUs. It suits streaming data where a compact running state is enough.

examples.input: Why do vanilla RNNs have vanishing or exploding gradients?
examples.output: Backpropagation through time multiplies the same recurrent Jacobian once per step; if its dominant scale is below one the product shrinks, above one it grows.

examples.input: What is shared across time steps?
examples.output: All weights and the bias; only the hidden state changes from step to step.

examples.input: How do gradient clipping and LSTMs help?
examples.output: Clipping bounds exploding gradients, while gated cells like the LSTM add an additive state path that lets gradients survive longer.

constraints: Hidden size H (memory capacity)
Number of stacked layers
Nonlinearity (tanh or ReLU)
Gradient clipping threshold
edgeCases: This card uses one bias; PyTorch keeps two (b_ih and b_hh) that simply add, so they must be summed when comparing
Shape mistakes are easy: weights are stored as (hidden, input) and applied transposed
Long sequences need clipping or gated cells to train stably

problems.title: ROC Curve and AUC
problems.summary: Sweep the decision threshold, plot true-positive rate against false-positive rate, and summarise the curve by its area (AUC).
problems.bruteForce: With heavy imbalance the false-positive rate hides many false alarms, so prefer a precision-recall curve. It also says nothing about calibration.
problems.intuition: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so it measures ranking quality and ignores calibration and the chosen threshold. A curve hugging the top-left corner means positives are almost always ranked above negatives.
problems.whyItWorks: Sorting by score and walking down the list, each positive moves the curve up and each negative moves it right. The area under that staircase counts, for every positive, the negatives ranked below it, which is the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by the number of positive-negative pairs.
approach: Sort samples by score, highest first — each prefix is one threshold
Cumulative sums of positives and negatives — give TP and FP at every cut
Keep only the last index of each tied score — tied samples cross the threshold together
Normalise by total positives and negatives — turns counts into TPR and FPR
Prepend the origin and integrate with trapezoids — the area is the AUC
problems.time: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep
problems.space: O(n)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def roc_curve(y, score):
    order = np.argsort(-score, kind="stable")
    y, s = y[order], score[order]
    tps = np.cumsum(y)
    fps = np.cumsum(1 - y)
    last = np.r_[np.where(np.diff(s))[0], len(s) - 1]
    tpr = np.r_[0, tps[last] / tps[-1]]
    fpr = np.r_[0, fps[last] / fps[-1]]
    return fpr, tpr

def auc(fpr, tpr):
    return np.sum(np.diff(fpr) * (tpr[1:] + tpr[:-1]) / 2)
dryRun: TPR = TP / (TP + FN),  FPR = FP / (FP + TN)
AUC = ∫ TPR d(FPR)
AUC = P(s⁺ > s⁻) + ½·P(s⁺ = s⁻)
AUC = U / (n₊ · n₋)
Trapezoid rule: Σ (Δfpr) · (tpr_i + tpr_{i−1}) / 2
problems.description: Comparing classifiers independent of threshold, or when the operating point is not yet known, and when classes are not extremely imbalanced.

examples.input: What is the probabilistic meaning of AUC?
examples.output: The chance that a random positive scores higher than a random negative, with ties counting half.

examples.input: Does AUC depend on calibration?
examples.output: No. Any monotonic transform of the scores leaves the ranking, and so the AUC, unchanged.

examples.input: When is PR-AUC better than ROC-AUC?
examples.output: When positives are rare: FPR stays small even with many false positives, while precision exposes them.

constraints: Positive class label (which class counts as positive)
Tie handling (tied scores are one threshold step)
Averaging for multiclass (one-vs-rest or one-vs-one, macro or weighted)
edgeCases: Needs both classes present, otherwise TPR or FPR is undefined
Treating tied scores as ordered inflates or deflates AUC
Optimistic on highly imbalanced data; check PR-AUC too
Using hard 0/1 predictions instead of scores collapses the curve to one point

problems.title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
problems.summary: Rotate each pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token position, so attention scores depend on relative offsets.
problems.bruteForce: Cases where absolute position matters more than offsets, or when the head width is odd. Beyond the trained length it needs rescaling methods to extrapolate.
problems.intuition: If you rotate a query by m·θ and a key by n·θ, their dot product depends only on the angle difference (m−n)·θ, because rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles. RoPE therefore injects relative position directly into the attention score with no learned position table, and each coordinate pair uses its own frequency so both short and long ranges are covered.
problems.whyItWorks: Treat each coordinate pair as a complex number; rotating by angle φ is multiplication by e^{iφ}. The score is the real part of the product of one rotated number and the conjugate of the other, so the two position angles combine into e^{i(m−n)θ}. The score is thus a function of the content vectors and the offset m−n alone, and rotations preserve norms so magnitudes are untouched.
approach: Pair up coordinates (x₀, x₁), (x₂, x₃), … — each pair is a point in a 2-D plane
Give pair i a frequency θᵢ = base^(−2i/d) — a spread of fast and slow rotations
Multiply position m by each θᵢ to get an angle — the angle grows linearly with position
Rotate every pair by its angle using cos and sin — a norm-preserving position encoding
Apply to queries and keys only, not values — only the score q·k needs relative position
problems.time: O(T·d) to rotate T vectors of width d
problems.space: O(T·d) for the rotated copy
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def rope(x, base=10000.0):
    T, d = x.shape
    theta = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    ang = np.arange(T)[:, None] * theta[None, :]
    cos, sin = np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0::2], x[:, 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[:, 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    out[:, 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out
dryRun: θᵢ = base^(−2i/d),   i = 0 … d/2 − 1
Pair i at position m: zᵢ = x₂ᵢ + i·x₂ᵢ₊₁
RoPE(x, m)ᵢ = zᵢ · e^{i·m·θᵢ}
(x′₂ᵢ, x′₂ᵢ₊₁) = R(mθᵢ)(x₂ᵢ, x₂ᵢ₊₁)
⟨RoPE(q, m), RoPE(k, n)⟩ = Re Σᵢ qᵢ · conj(kᵢ) · e^{i(m−n)θᵢ}
problems.description: Decoder language models and long-context models that want relative position information without a learned table; used in many open LLMs.

examples.input: Why does RoPE give relative position?
examples.output: Rotations compose by adding angles and preserve dot products, so the query-key score depends on the rotation by m−n and not on m and n separately.

examples.input: Why rotate only queries and keys?
examples.output: Position needs to enter the attention score q·k. Values are just averaged, so rotating them would corrupt the content being passed along.

examples.input: How does RoPE differ from sinusoidal positional encoding?
examples.output: Sinusoidal encoding is added to the embeddings once at the input. RoPE multiplies q and k by rotations inside every attention layer and adds no parameters.

constraints: Frequency base (larger bases favour longer contexts)
Head width d (must be even)
Position scaling factor for context extension
edgeCases: Pairing convention differs between libraries (adjacent pairs here, split halves in others); weights are not interchangeable
Apply it per head, to q and k after the projection and before the dot product
In float16 the angles for large positions lose precision; compute cos and sin in float32

problems.title: ROUGE-N and ROUGE-L
problems.summary: Score a generated summary against a reference by n-gram overlap (ROUGE-N) or by the longest common subsequence of words (ROUGE-L), reported as precision, recall and F1.
problems.bruteForce: Abstractive outputs that paraphrase the reference, where overlap understates quality, and tasks where factual correctness matters more than wording. It cannot detect hallucinations that reuse the reference's words.
problems.intuition: ROUGE asks how much of the reference the candidate recovered, which is recall, and the F1 version also asks how much of the candidate was actually in the reference. ROUGE-N counts exact n-gram matches and is strict about local phrasing; ROUGE-L only needs the shared words to appear in the same order, with gaps allowed, so it rewards keeping the reference's sequence without demanding adjacency.
problems.whyItWorks: Summaries should contain the reference's key content, and overlap of words and phrases is a cheap proxy for that. Clipped counts (the multiset intersection) stop repeated words from inflating the score. The longest common subsequence is found by dynamic programming over prefixes, because the best match of two prefixes extends the best match of shorter prefixes.
approach: Tokenise candidate and reference the same way — scores are only comparable under one tokenisation
ROUGE-N: count n-grams in each and intersect the counts — clipped overlap, so repeats do not inflate the score
ROUGE-L: fill the LCS table over word prefixes — finds the longest in-order, gap-tolerant match
Divide the overlap by candidate length for precision and by reference length for recall — ROUGE is usually quoted as recall, F1 balances both
Combine into F1 — a single number that penalises both padding and omission
problems.time: ROUGE-N O(m + n); ROUGE-L O(m·n) for candidate length m and reference length n
problems.space: O(m·n) for the LCS table (O(min(m, n)) with a rolling row)
dryRun: overlap = Σ_g min(count_cand(g), count_ref(g))  over n-grams g
P = overlap / (n-grams in candidate)
R = overlap / (n-grams in reference)
F₁ = 2PR / (P + R)
LCS DP: L[i,j] = L[i−1,j−1] + 1 if aᵢ = bⱼ
else max(L[i−1,j], L[i,j−1])
ROUGE-L: overlap = L[|cand|, |ref|], then P, R, F₁ as above
problems.description: Comparing summarisation or headline-generation systems when a reference is available, using a standard package so tokenisation and stemming match published numbers.

examples.input: Why is ROUGE recall-oriented while BLEU is precision-oriented?
examples.output: Summarisation asks whether the key reference content was captured, which is recall. Translation asks whether what was produced is correct, which is precision, with a brevity penalty. Modern ROUGE reports all three.

examples.input: How does ROUGE-L differ from ROUGE-2?
examples.output: ROUGE-2 needs adjacent word pairs to match exactly. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence, so matched words must be in the same order but may have other words between them.

examples.input: How is the longest common subsequence computed?
examples.output: Dynamic programming over prefixes: if the last words match, extend the diagonal cell by one; otherwise take the larger of dropping the last word of either sequence.

constraints: N-gram order N (ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 are most common)
Variant (ROUGE-N, ROUGE-L sentence level, ROUGE-Lsum summary level)
Stemming and stop-word handling
Which statistic to report: precision, recall or F1
edgeCases: Tokenisation and stemming change the score; use one package for all systems
This ROUGE-L is sentence level; the summary-level ROUGE-Lsum splits sentences and unions LCS matches
This code takes one reference and tokens already split, lower-cased and unstemmed
High overlap does not imply factual correctness or fluency

problems.title: Self-Attention
problems.summary: Let every token build its output as a weighted average of all tokens' values, with weights from how well its query matches each token's key.
problems.bruteForce: Cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so very long inputs need sparse, linear or chunked variants. It also has no built-in notion of order and needs positional information.
problems.intuition: Each token asks a question (query), and every token advertises what it holds (key) and what it would contribute (value). A softmax over query-key similarity turns the match scores into mixing weights, so information moves directly between any two positions in one step, regardless of distance.
problems.whyItWorks: Content-based weights let the model decide at run time which tokens matter to each other, and a single layer connects all pairs, so long range dependencies need no recurrence. Dividing scores by $\sqrt{d}$ keeps their variance from growing with dimension, which would otherwise push softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients.
approach: Project $X$ into queries, keys and values — separate roles for asking, matching and contributing
Compute scores $QK^{\top}$ and divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$ — similarity of every pair, scaled to keep softmax healthy
Mask future positions with $-\infty$ if causal — stops a token from seeing what it must predict
Softmax each row — turns scores into weights that sum to one
Multiply the weights by $V$ — each output is a weighted average of values
problems.time: O(T²·d) for sequence length T and width d
problems.space: O(T²) for the attention matrix
dryRun: Q = XW_q,  K = XW_k,  V = XW_v   (X: T × d)
S = QKᵀ / √d_k
Causal: set S[i, j] = −∞ for j > i
A = softmax(S) row-wise
Output = A·V
problems.description: Language, vision transformers, and any set or sequence where relations between arbitrary positions matter and sequence length is moderate.

examples.input: Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
examples.output: Dot products of $d_k$-dimensional vectors have variance growing with $d_k$; scaling keeps scores in a range where softmax gradients stay useful.

examples.input: What is the difference between self- and cross-attention?
examples.output: In self-attention queries, keys and values come from the same sequence; in cross-attention queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another.

examples.input: Why does a decoder need a causal mask?
examples.output: So position $i$ attends only to positions up to $i$, which keeps training consistent with left-to-right generation.

constraints: Key/query dimension $d_k$ (sets the scale $\sqrt{d_k}$)
Number of heads (this code is one head)
Causal masking on or off
Attention dropout
edgeCases: Forgetting the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling saturates the softmax
A fully masked row gives NaN with $-\infty$; causal masks always keep the diagonal
Without positional encodings the layer is permutation-equivariant
Quadratic memory limits sequence length

problems.title: Silhouette, ARI and NMI
problems.summary: Three ways to score a clustering. The silhouette needs only the data and the labels and measures cohesion against separation; the adjusted Rand index and normalised mutual information compare two labelings, for example clusters against ground truth.
problems.bruteForce: Skip silhouette for non-convex clusters such as rings, where it favours convex shapes; NMI is biased toward many clusters unless adjusted, and none of these show whether clusters are useful for your task.
problems.intuition: Cluster labels are arbitrary names, so a good score must not depend on which number is called which. The silhouette asks whether each point is closer to its own cluster than to the next one; ARI and NMI ask whether two labelings group the same pairs together, after subtracting what random labelings would score by chance (ARI) or normalising the shared information (NMI).
problems.whyItWorks: Both external scores are computed from the contingency table of label pairs, which is invariant to renaming clusters. ARI corrects the pair counting for chance agreement so random labelings score near zero, and NMI divides the mutual information by the entropies so the scale is fixed between 0 and 1.
approach: Silhouette: take all pairwise distances — every score is built from them
For each point average the distance to its own cluster and to each other cluster — cohesion a and separation b
Combine as (b − a) / max(a, b) and average — near 1 well separated, near 0 on a boundary, negative misassigned
ARI and NMI: build the contingency table of the two labelings — the only thing both scores depend on
ARI counts agreeing pairs and subtracts the chance expectation — chance labelings score about zero
NMI computes mutual information and divides by the average entropy — a bounded, label-name-free score
problems.time: O(n²·d) for the silhouette, O(n + kᵤ·kᵥ) for ARI and NMI once the table is built
problems.space: O(n²) for the distance matrix, O(kᵤ·kᵥ) for the contingency table
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def silhouette(X, y):
    D = np.sqrt(((X[:, None] - X[None]) ** 2).sum(-1))
    s = []
    for i in range(len(X)):
        own = y == y[i]
        if own.sum() == 1:
            s.append(0.0)
            continue
        a = D[i, own].sum() / (own.sum() - 1)
        b = min(D[i, y == c].mean() for c in set(y) - {y[i]})
        s.append((b - a) / max(a, b))
    return np.mean(s)

def table(u, v):
    iu = np.unique(u, return_inverse=True)[1]
    iv = np.unique(v, return_inverse=True)[1]
    C = np.zeros((iu.max() + 1, iv.max() + 1))
    np.add.at(C, (iu, iv), 1)
    return C

def ari(u, v):
    C, n = table(u, v), len(u)
    c2 = lambda x: (x * (x - 1) / 2).sum()
    s, sa, sb = c2(C), c2(C.sum(1)), c2(C.sum(0))
    e = sa * sb / c2(np.array(n))
    return (s - e) / ((sa + sb) / 2 - e)

def nmi(u, v):
    P = table(u, v) / len(u)
    pa, pb = P.sum(1), P.sum(0)
    nz = P > 0
    mi = (P[nz] * np.log(P[nz] / np.outer(pa, pb)[nz])).sum()
    h = lambda p: -(p[p > 0] * np.log(p[p > 0])).sum()
    return mi / ((h(pa) + h(pb)) / 2)
dryRun: aᵢ = mean distance to the other points in i's cluster
bᵢ = smallest mean distance from i to another cluster
sᵢ = (bᵢ − aᵢ) / max(aᵢ, bᵢ),  score = mean of sᵢ
Contingency nᵢⱼ = #points in cluster i of U and j of V
ARI = (Σ C(nᵢⱼ,2) − E) / (½[ΣC(aᵢ,2) + ΣC(bⱼ,2)] − E)
E = ΣC(aᵢ,2) · ΣC(bⱼ,2) / C(n,2)
MI = Σ pᵢⱼ log(pᵢⱼ / (pᵢ pⱼ)),  NMI = MI / ((H(U) + H(V)) / 2)
problems.description: Silhouette to compare values of k or algorithms without labels, ARI and NMI when reference classes exist, and benchmarking clustering methods on labelled datasets.

examples.input: How do you read a silhouette value?
examples.output: Near +1 the point is far from other clusters and close to its own, near 0 it sits between two clusters, and negative values suggest it was assigned to the wrong cluster.

examples.input: Why use ARI instead of the plain Rand index?
examples.output: The Rand index is high even for random labelings when there are many clusters; ARI subtracts the expected chance agreement so random labelings score near zero.

examples.input: How is NMI different from accuracy for clustering?
examples.output: NMI does not need cluster ids to match class ids; it measures shared information between the two partitions, so permuting cluster names leaves it unchanged.

constraints: Distance metric for the silhouette — Euclidean by default, must match the clustering
NMI normaliser — arithmetic, geometric, min or max of the two entropies
Sampling — compute the silhouette on a subsample for large n
edgeCases: Silhouette is undefined for a single cluster and this code assumes at least two
Silhouette prefers convex, evenly dense clusters and can rank a poor k-means above a correct density clustering
NMI (unadjusted) tends to rise as the number of clusters grows
ARI and NMI assume the ground-truth classes are the right notion of cluster

problems.title: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
problems.summary: Turn a vector of raw class scores (logits) into probabilities with softmax, then score them with the negative log-probability of the true class.
problems.bruteForce: Not for multi-label tasks where several classes can be true at once (use per-class sigmoids with binary cross-entropy), nor for regression targets.
problems.intuition: Softmax makes the classes compete: raising one logit steals probability from all the others. Cross-entropy then only looks at the probability given to the correct class, and its gradient with respect to the logits collapses to the simple form p − y, so wrong and confident predictions get the strongest push.
problems.whyItWorks: Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical distribution, so minimising it is maximum-likelihood training. The log cancels the exponential in softmax, leaving the clean gradient p − onehot(y) that does not vanish when the model is wrong, unlike squared error.
approach: Subtract each row's max from its logits — stops exp from overflowing
Exponentiate and normalise by the row sum — gives a probability per class
Compute log Σ exp(z) − z_y per row and average — the loss, via log-sum-exp so no log(0)
For the gradient, subtract 1 at the true class from p and divide by n — it is the exact derivative w.r.t. logits
problems.time: O(n·k) for n samples and k classes
problems.space: O(n·k) for the probability matrix
dryRun: softmax(z)ᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ)
Stable form: subtract max(z) from z before exp (result unchanged)
CE = −log p_y = −z_y + log Σⱼ exp(zⱼ)
∂CE/∂zᵢ = pᵢ − 1[i = y]
Batch loss: mean over rows; gradient divided by batch size n
problems.description: The default output layer and loss for single-label multi-class classification in neural networks and for multinomial logistic regression.

examples.input: Why is the softmax and cross-entropy gradient just p − y?
examples.output: The log in cross-entropy cancels the exponential in softmax, leaving the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target.

examples.input: Why subtract the max before exp?
examples.output: Softmax is shift-invariant, so it changes nothing mathematically but prevents overflow.

examples.input: Should a PyTorch model end in softmax before CrossEntropyLoss?
examples.output: No. CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits and applies log-softmax internally.

constraints: Label smoothing (softens the one-hot target to reduce overconfidence)
Temperature (divides logits; higher is flatter, lower is sharper)
Class weights (rescale the loss for imbalanced classes)
edgeCases: Naive exp overflows for large logits; always subtract the row max
Taking log of softmax in two steps loses precision; use log-sum-exp
Applying softmax then a framework CrossEntropyLoss applies it twice
Outputs are confident but not necessarily calibrated

problems.title: Stratified Train/Test Split
problems.summary: Split data by shuffling and sampling each class separately so train and test keep (almost) the same class proportions as the full dataset.
problems.bruteForce: Time series or grouped data, where the split must respect time order or keep groups together instead (use a temporal or group split); also regression targets unless you bin them first.
problems.intuition: A purely random split of an imbalanced dataset can, by bad luck, put too few or even zero minority samples in the test set, making the metric noisy or undefined. Sampling the same fraction from each class removes that source of variance: every class appears in test in proportion to its overall share, up to rounding.
problems.whyItWorks: Random sampling gives test class counts that vary like a hypergeometric draw, which is noisy for small classes. Stratifying fixes each class's test count by design, so only rounding remains and the class proportions in train and test differ from the population by at most a single sample per class. This lowers the variance of the evaluation without introducing bias for the overall population.
approach: Seed a random generator — makes the split reproducible
For each class, shuffle the indices of that class — random choice within the class
Take the first round(f · n_c) shuffled indices for test — same fraction from every class
Collect test indices, then train is the complement — a clean partition with no overlap
Check proportions in both parts — confirms the stratification worked
problems.time: O(n) plus shuffling each class
problems.space: O(n) for the index arrays
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def stratified_split(y, test_frac=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    test = []
    for c in np.unique(y):
        idx = rng.permutation(np.flatnonzero(y == c))
        k = int(round(test_frac * len(idx)))
        test.extend(idx[:k])
    test = np.array(sorted(test))
    train = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), test)
    return train, test
dryRun: Class share: π_c = n_c / n
Test count per class: k_c = round(f · n_c)
Test set T = ∪_c (k_c random indices of class c), train = rest
Proportion gap: | k_c/|T| − π_c | stays within rounding of f·n_c
Unstratified: k_c ~ Hypergeometric, var > 0 for small n_c
problems.description: Classification with imbalanced or small classes, small datasets where one rare sample matters, and cross-validation folds (stratified k-fold).

examples.input: Why stratify?
examples.output: It keeps class proportions the same in train and test, so rare classes are represented in evaluation and metrics have lower variance.

examples.input: Does stratifying introduce bias?
examples.output: No for population-level estimates: each sample still has the same inclusion probability within its class, and the only change is removing class-count variance.

examples.input: When is stratifying the wrong tool?
examples.output: For temporal or grouped data, where you must split by time or by group to avoid leakage, and for continuous targets unless they are binned.

examples.input: How do you stratify on several columns?
examples.output: Combine them into one composite label (for example class and region) and stratify on that, making sure each combination has enough samples.

constraints: test_frac — fraction held out
seed — fixes the shuffle for reproducibility
stratify target — the label (or a combined label or binned target)
edgeCases: Per-class rounding can make the total test size differ slightly from f·n; sklearn allocates counts to hit it exactly, so splits are close but not identical
A class with a single sample cannot appear in both parts; sklearn raises an error here, this code silently keeps it in train
Stratifying does not fix leakage: duplicates or related rows can still straddle the split
Split before preprocessing or feature selection, otherwise test statistics leak into training

problems.title: Singular Value Decomposition
problems.summary: Every matrix factors as A = U S Vᵀ with orthonormal U and V and non-negative singular values in S. Keeping only the largest few gives the best low-rank approximation of A.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a full SVD for huge sparse matrices (use truncated or randomised methods) and when missing entries need handling, since SVD needs a fully observed matrix. The eigen-route in the code squares the condition number, so use a library SVD in production.
problems.intuition: A matrix maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid. The SVD names the ellipsoid's axes: V gives the input directions, the singular values give how much each is stretched, and U gives the output directions. Directions with tiny stretch contribute almost nothing, so you can drop them and keep a compact matrix that behaves nearly the same.
problems.whyItWorks: AᵀA = V S² Vᵀ, so the right singular vectors are eigenvectors of AᵀA and the singular values are the square roots of its eigenvalues. The Eckart-Young theorem says that, in both the Frobenius and spectral norms, no rank-k matrix is closer to A than the truncation that keeps the top k singular triplets, and the error is set by the discarded singular values.
approach: Form AᵀA — its eigenvectors are the right singular vectors
Eigendecompose it and sort eigenvalues in decreasing order — singular values are conventionally ordered
Take square roots (clipping tiny negatives from rounding) — gives the singular values
Compute U = A V / s column by column — the left vectors follow from the right ones
Truncate to the top k triplets for a low-rank approximation — Eckart-Young says this is optimal
problems.time: O(m·n²) for AᵀA plus O(n³) for the eigen step (m ≥ n); library SVD is similar but more stable
problems.space: O(m·n) for the matrices and O(n²) for AᵀA
dryRun: A = U S Vᵀ,  UᵀU = I,  VᵀV = I,  s₁ ≥ s₂ ≥ … ≥ 0
AᵀA = V S² Vᵀ  (eigendecomposition)
uᵢ = A vᵢ / sᵢ
Rank-k truncation: A_k = Σ_{i≤k} sᵢ uᵢ vᵢᵀ
‖A − A_k‖_F² = Σ_{i>k} sᵢ²
problems.description: PCA, low-rank compression, denoising, latent semantic analysis, recommender factorisation, pseudo-inverses and least squares on ill-conditioned problems.

examples.input: How does SVD relate to eigendecomposition?
examples.output: The right singular vectors are the eigenvectors of AᵀA and the left ones those of AAᵀ, with singular values the square roots of the shared non-zero eigenvalues.

examples.input: What does the Eckart-Young theorem say?
examples.output: Truncating the SVD to rank k gives the closest rank-k matrix to A in the spectral and Frobenius norms.

examples.input: How is SVD used in PCA?
examples.output: Centre the data, take its SVD, and the right singular vectors are the principal axes while squared singular values over n − 1 are the variances.

examples.input: Why is SVD better than the normal equations for least squares?
examples.output: It works with A directly, avoiding the squared condition number of AᵀA, and gives a stable pseudo-inverse for rank-deficient problems.

constraints: Rank k — chosen from the singular-value spectrum or an energy target
Full or thin (economy) factorisation
Solver — full, truncated or randomised
edgeCases: This code assumes m ≥ n and nonzero singular values; zero ones leave zero columns in U
Forming AᵀA squares the condition number and loses accuracy for small singular values
Singular vectors are only defined up to a joint sign flip, and are unstable when singular values are close
SVD of uncentred data is not PCA; centre the columns first

problems.title: Support Vector Machine
problems.summary: Find the separating hyperplane with the widest margin. The code is a simplified linear soft-margin SVM trained by full-batch sub-gradient descent on the hinge loss; kernels and the dual solver (SMO) are not implemented.
problems.bruteForce: Skip kernel SVMs on very large datasets (training scales badly with n), when you need probabilities directly, or when classes overlap heavily and features are unscaled.
problems.intuition: Many hyperplanes separate two classes, but the one farthest from both is least likely to be thrown off by new points. Only the points on or inside the margin matter for the solution (the support vectors), so confidently classified points are simply ignored.
problems.whyItWorks: The hinge loss max(0, 1 − y·f) is zero for points beyond the margin, so they give no gradient, and the ‖w‖² term maximises the margin 2/‖w‖. The objective is convex, so sub-gradient descent with a decaying step converges to the global optimum, the same one the dual quadratic program finds.
approach: Encode labels as −1/+1 — so y·f > 0 means correct
Find points with y·f(x) < 1 — only margin violators contribute to the gradient
Sum their yx terms and add λw — hinge sub-gradient plus margin regulariser
Take a step with size 1/(λ(t + 10)) — a decaying step gives convergence
Repeat for many iterations — then classify with sign(wᵀx + b)
problems.time: O(iters · n · d) here; kernel SVM solvers are between O(n²) and O(n³)
problems.space: O(n · d) for the data; kernel SVMs also store the support vectors
dryRun: f(x) = wᵀx + b,  ŷ = sign f(x),  y ∈ {−1, +1}
Margin width = 2 / ‖w‖
min ½λ‖w‖² + (1/n) Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ f(xᵢ))
Violators V = {i : yᵢ f(xᵢ) < 1}
∂w = λw − (1/n) Σ_{i∈V} yᵢ xᵢ
Step size ηₜ = 1 / (λ(t + 10))
Equivalent to sklearn C = 1 / (λ n)
problems.description: Medium-sized, high-dimensional problems (text, genomics) with a clear margin, and with a kernel when the boundary is curved.

examples.input: What are support vectors?
examples.output: The training points on or inside the margin; they alone determine the hyperplane and removing any other point leaves it unchanged.

examples.input: What does C control?
examples.output: The penalty on margin violations: large C tolerates few violations (narrow margin, low bias), small C allows more (wide margin, more regularisation).

examples.input: What is the kernel trick?
examples.output: The dual problem uses only dot products xᵢ·xⱼ, so replacing them with a kernel k(xᵢ, xⱼ) gives a linear margin in an implicit high-dimensional space without computing it.

constraints: C (or λ = 1/(C·n)) — large C fits training data harder, small C widens the margin
kernel — linear, RBF, polynomial
gamma — RBF width; large values overfit
Feature scaling — required, since the margin is distance-based
edgeCases: Unscaled features let one large feature dominate the margin
Scores are not probabilities; Platt scaling is needed
RBF with a large gamma memorises the training set
This card's code is linear only and uses sub-gradient descent instead of the dual solver

problems.title: TF-IDF
problems.summary: Represent each document as a vector of word counts, rescaled so that words found in few documents count more than words found everywhere.
problems.bruteForce: It ignores word order and meaning, so synonyms look unrelated. Prefer learned embeddings or transformers when semantics matter, and note that idf must be fitted on training data only.
problems.intuition: A word that appears in nearly every document says little about any one of them, while a word concentrated in a few documents is a strong signature. Multiplying the term count by the log of inverse document frequency keeps the frequent-here, rare-elsewhere words and mutes filler such as "the".
problems.whyItWorks: The idf term is the log of how surprising it is to find a word in a random document, so it is a cheap information weight. Smoothing adds one to the counts so unseen words never divide by zero, and L2 normalisation makes the dot product of two rows their cosine similarity, independent of document length.
approach: Build a vocabulary and count terms per document — gives the raw tf matrix
Count in how many documents each term occurs — this is df
Compute idf with add-one smoothing — rare terms get larger weights, no division by zero
Multiply tf by idf column-wise — reweights each term by informativeness
Normalise each row to unit L2 length — removes the effect of document length
problems.time: O(total tokens) to count, O(N·V) for the dense weighting
problems.space: O(N·V) dense here; real systems use sparse matrices
dryRun: tf(t,d) = count of term t in document d
df(t) = number of documents containing t
idf(t) = ln((1 + N) / (1 + df(t))) + 1   (smooth form)
x(t,d) = tf(t,d) · idf(t)
Row norm: x(d) ← x(d) / ‖x(d)‖₂
Cosine similarity of two rows = their dot product after L2 norm
problems.description: Strong, fast baseline features for text classification, search ranking and document similarity, especially with linear models and small datasets.

examples.input: Why take the log in idf?
examples.output: It damps the ratio N/df so that a very rare word does not dominate, and it makes the weight behave like an information measure.

examples.input: Why normalise rows?
examples.output: Long documents have larger counts. L2 normalisation makes rows comparable and turns the dot product into cosine similarity.

examples.input: How does TF-IDF differ from word embeddings?
examples.output: TF-IDF vectors are sparse, one dimension per word, and carry no notion of meaning. Embeddings are dense and learned so similar words lie close together.

constraints: smooth_idf (add one to document counts, as here)
sublinear_tf (use 1 + ln(tf) so repeats saturate)
norm (l2 for cosine similarity, l1, or none)
min_df / max_df (drop very rare or very common terms)
n-gram range (include word pairs to recover some order)
edgeCases: Fitting idf on the full dataset leaks test statistics into training
This sketch splits on spaces only; real tokenisation handles case and punctuation
The dense matrix is huge for real vocabularies; use sparse storage
Variants differ (log base, smoothing, norm), so scores are not portable between libraries

problems.title: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
problems.summary: Truncate the next-token distribution to the k most likely tokens, or to the smallest set whose probability reaches p, then renormalise and sample from what is left.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks with one right answer, such as translation or code, where greedy or beam search is better, and likelihood evaluation, where the full distribution must be used.
problems.intuition: Sampling from the full distribution occasionally picks a token from the long, unreliable tail and derails the text, while greedy decoding is repetitive. Cutting the tail removes the junk and keeps real randomness among plausible tokens; top-p adapts the cut to the model's confidence, keeping few tokens when it is sure and many when it is not.
problems.whyItWorks: Truncation sets the probability of unreliable tail tokens to exactly zero while keeping the relative odds among the survivors after renormalising. Top-p measures the cut in probability mass rather than token count, so the candidate set shrinks when the distribution is peaked and grows when it is flat. The token that crosses the threshold is kept, so the nucleus is never empty.
approach: Sort tokens by logit, highest first — fixes the order used for both cuts
Top-k: set every logit beyond the k-th to −∞ — keeps a fixed number of candidates
Softmax the survivors and take cumulative sums — the mass collected so far
Top-p: drop a token once the mass before it is at least p — keeps the smallest nucleus reaching p
Sample from the renormalised survivors — the softmax gives zero weight to −∞
problems.time: O(V log V) for the sort over vocabulary size V
problems.space: O(V) for the filtered logits
dryRun: pᵢ = exp(zᵢ / τ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ / τ)
Top-k: keep i if rank(i) ≤ k
Sort p₍₁₎ ≥ p₍₂₎ ≥ …; cumulative Cⱼ = Σ_{m ≤ j} p₍ₘ₎
Top-p: keep rank j if Cⱼ₋₁ < p   (C₀ = 0)
p′ᵢ = pᵢ · 1[kept] / Σⱼ pⱼ · 1[kept]
problems.description: Open-ended generation such as chat, stories and brainstorming, where diversity is wanted but low-probability tokens cause incoherence.

examples.input: How does top-p differ from top-k?
examples.output: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the distribution looks like. Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching probability mass p, so its size adapts to how confident the model is.

examples.input: Why renormalise after truncating?
examples.output: The kept probabilities no longer sum to one. The softmax over the remaining logits rescales them so the sample is drawn from a valid distribution.

examples.input: What does temperature do and in what order is it applied?
examples.output: It divides the logits before the softmax; low values sharpen and high values flatten the distribution. It is normally applied first, then the truncation.

constraints: Top-k (0 disables)
Top-p threshold in (0, 1]
Temperature τ
Order of temperature, top-k and top-p
edgeCases: Libraries differ on whether top-p uses the distribution before or after top-k; here top-p sees the renormalised top-k survivors
top_p = 0 would drop every token; use a value above zero
Ties at the cut are broken by sort order, so which tied token is kept is arbitrary

problems.title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
problems.summary: Start from a network pretrained on a large dataset, freeze some of its layers and train the rest, usually a new output head, on your small task.
problems.bruteForce: When the target domain is very different from the pretraining data and you have lots of data, training from scratch or unfreezing most layers may fit better. Frozen features also carry the pretraining biases.
problems.intuition: Early layers of a network trained on a big dataset learn generic features such as edges and textures that are useful for many tasks. Keeping them frozen reuses that knowledge and leaves very few parameters to fit on your small dataset, so the model overfits less and trains faster. Unfreezing more layers with a small learning rate lets the features adapt when the new task differs more.
problems.whyItWorks: A pretrained network is a strong prior in weight space, far better than random initialisation when data is scarce. Freezing means no gradient flows into those weights, so they stay at the prior, and only the head has to learn the task-specific mapping on top of fixed features.
approach: Run the forward pass through backbone and head — gives logits and the activations needed later
Compute the output error p − y — the starting signal for backpropagation
Always compute the head gradient — the head is the part being trained
Compute the backbone gradient only if it is not frozen — skipping it saves compute and keeps weights fixed
Update only parameters that received a gradient — frozen weights never change
problems.time: O(N·(D·H + H·K)) forward; the backbone backward is skipped when frozen
problems.space: O(N·H) activations plus gradients only for trainable weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def finetune_step(params, x, y, lr, frozen=()):
    W1, W2 = params["W1"], params["W2"]
    h = np.maximum(x @ W1, 0)
    z = h @ W2
    p = np.exp(z - z.max(1, keepdims=True))
    p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    p[np.arange(len(y)), y] -= 1
    dz = p / len(y)
    grads = {}
    if "W2" not in frozen:
        grads["W2"] = h.T @ dz
    if "W1" not in frozen:
        grads["W1"] = x.T @ ((dz @ W2.T) * (h > 0))
    new = dict(params)
    for k, g in grads.items():
        new[k] = params[k] - lr * g
    return new, grads
dryRun: Features h = relu(x W₁),  logits z = h W₂
Loss L = CE(softmax(z), y)
Head gradient: ∂L/∂W₂ = hᵀ · (p − y) / N
Backbone gradient: ∂L/∂W₁ = xᵀ · (((p − y) W₂ᵀ) ⊙ 1[h > 0]) / N
Frozen set F: update w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w only for w ∉ F
problems.description: Small labelled datasets in a domain related to a large pretraining set, such as images, text or audio with a public pretrained model.

examples.input: What is the difference between feature extraction and fine-tuning?
examples.output: Feature extraction freezes the whole backbone and trains only a new head; fine-tuning also updates some or all backbone weights.

examples.input: Why use a smaller learning rate for pretrained layers?
examples.output: Their weights are already good, so small steps adapt them without erasing the pretrained features.

examples.input: When does freezing help most?
examples.output: When the target dataset is small and similar to the pretraining data, so fixed features are good and few parameters need fitting.

constraints: Which layers to freeze (and when to unfreeze)
Learning rate (smaller for pretrained layers than for the new head)
Head architecture
Number of fine-tuning epochs

A large learning rate on pretrained layers destroys the features it should keep
